nodes.title: Annotations
nodes.summary: Structured metadata attached to constructs with @tag annotations, declared with annotation declarations and readable at runtime through typedesc values.

must_cover.text: Attach annotations such as `@marker`, `@info {label: "Name"}` or the qualified `@mod:config {...}` in a construct's metadata (after any documentation string), with several annotations allowed on one construct

Declare annotation tags with `annotation Info info on function;` (optionally `public` and `const`), knowing annotation tags live in their own symbol space, separate from other module declarations and from module and XML namespace prefixes

Explain that an annotation tag's type must be a subtype of `true`, `map<value:Cloneable>` or `map<value:Cloneable>[]`, defaulting to `true` when omitted, and that a `true`-typed annotation cannot take a mapping value

Explain that when a tag's type is `M[]` the annotation may be applied several times and its effective value is an array of the values; otherwise only one annotation with that tag is allowed on a construct

Explain that an omitted annotation value defaults to `{}` for mapping-typed tags, that the mapping constructor is evaluated with the tag's mapping type as the contextually expected type, and that the result has ImmutableClone applied

Restrict where a tag may be used with attachment points: `type`, `class`, `function`, `object function`, `service remote function`, `return`, `parameter`, `service`, `field`, `object field`, `record field`, and the source-only `annotation`, `external`, `var`, `const`, `listener`, `client` and `worker`
Explain that an attachment point prefixed with `source` attaches the annotation to the source fragment only (not available at runtime), and that the annotation declaration must then be `const`
Explain that for a `const` annotation tag the value must be a const-expr evaluated at compile time, whereas other annotation values are evaluated at runtime

Explain when annotations are evaluated: those on module-level declarations during module initialization, those on a service constructor when it is evaluated, and those inside a type descriptor when it is resolved
Read an annotation at runtime with the annotation access expression `t.@tag`, where `t` is a `typedesc`, which yields the annotation value or `()` and has static type `T?`

Explain which type descriptor a non-source annotation is attached to at runtime: the defined type for `type` and `class`, the function's type for `function`, `return` and `parameter`, and the containing mapping, list or object type for fields

Explain that an unqualified annotation tag reference does not refer to a tag declared in the same module; the compilation environment decides which unqualified tags exist and which module defines them, while a qualified reference resolves through an import
Use a type cast containing only annotations, `<@tag {...}> expr`, whose only effect is to add the annotations to the contextually expected type of `expr`

nodes.notes: The source-only-attach-point grammar includes `client`, but the attachment-point table in 9.1 has no `client` row, so what it attaches to is unclear. 9.1 also says 'annotation-tag-reference' where the grammar says 'annot-tag-reference'.

nodes.title: Arithmetic operators
nodes.summary: Unary, multiplicative, additive, shift and binary bitwise operators, their per-type semantics including overflow panics, and nil lifting.

must_cover.text: Use unary `+`, `-` (negation) and `~` (bitwise complement, int only), knowing int negation panics on overflow for `int:MIN_VALUE` and float/decimal negation is the IEEE negate operation, not subtraction from zero
Explain that int `+`, `-` and `*` panic on overflow instead of wrapping around
Explain that int `/` truncates toward zero and panics on division by zero and on `int:MIN_VALUE / -1`
Explain that int `%` is consistent with truncating division so `(x/y)*y + (x%y) == x`, panics when the divisor is zero, and returns 0 for `int:MIN_VALUE % -1`

Explain that float `+`, `-`, `*` and `/` perform the IEEE 754-2008 operations with the same destination format and never panic, and that decimal arithmetic likewise uses the IEEE decimal operations with roundTiesToEven

Explain floating `%` semantics: it is not the IEEE remainder but x - y*n rounded, with n the quotient truncated toward zero and a zero result taking the sign of x; it is NaN when x is NaN or infinite or y is NaN or zero, and it returns x for finite x and infinite y

Use int operands with float or decimal operands in multiplicative expressions only when the second operand is int, or the operator is `*` and the first is int; the int is converted to the other operand's type (e.g. `2.5 * 2`, `d / 3`)
Explain that `x / 0.0` with a singleton float `0.0` divisor has static type `float` rather than a singleton, because `0.0 == -0.0` but `1.0/0.0 != 1.0/-0.0`
Explain that `+` and `-` require both operands of the same basic type (int, float, decimal, string or xml for `+`), or one xml and one string for `+`, so `int + float` is a compile error
Use `+` to concatenate strings, xml values (without copying constituents), or xml with string, where an empty string leaves the xml unchanged and a non-empty string becomes an xml text item
Use `<<`, `>>` (sign-propagating) and `>>>` (zero-filling) on ints, knowing only the bottom 6 bits of the shift amount are used (as if masked with `0x3F`)
Explain that `>>` and `>>>` applied to a left operand of type `int:Unsigned8`, `int:Unsigned16` or `int:Unsigned32` produce that smallest unsigned type, otherwise `int`
Use `&`, `^` and `|` on ints, knowing `&` yields `int:UnsignedN` if either operand is an unsigned subtype while `^` and `|` need both operands unsigned to do so
Apply nil lifting so arithmetic, shift and bitwise operators accept optional operands (e.g. `int? a; a + 1`), returning nil if any operand is nil and giving a result of type `T?`

Explain that the contextually expected type of an arithmetic expression is passed to its operands restricted to numeric (and for `+`, string and xml) basic types, so `decimal d = 1.5 * 2.0;` types the literals as decimal

nodes.notes: Possible inconsistency: 5.2.4.2 says decimal operations that would yield NaN, infinity or a subnormal panic, whereas 6.23/6.24 say float and decimal `*`, `/`, `+`, `-` 'never' cause a panic (e.g. decimal division by zero). Items avoid asserting either for decimal division by zero; flag for review. The int negation overflow text reads '-263)' which is -2^63. Spec text for `%` on floats says n is the integer nearest the quotient 'without exceeding it in magnitude' (truncation).

nodes.title: Arrays and tuples
nodes.summary: List values described by array types (one member type, optional fixed length) and tuple types (a type per member, optional rest), built with list constructors.

must_cover.text: Declare arrays with `T[]`, build them with list constructors `[a, b, c]`, read members with `arr[i]` and get the length with `arr.length()`
Declare fixed-length arrays `T[n]` where n is an int literal or a reference to a non-negative int constant, and explain that `T[n]` is a subtype of `T[]`
Use `T[*]` to infer the array length from the initializer, and know it is allowed only in local or module variable declarations with an initializer and in constant declarations
Declare and index multidimensional arrays such as `int[3][4]`, where the dimension order in the type matches the index order in `v[i][j]`
Define tuple types such as `[int, string]` with a separate type for each member, and know that a tuple with all members the same type and no rest descriptor is equivalent to a fixed-length array
Use tuple rest descriptors such as `[int, string...]` and `[T...]` to allow a variable number of trailing members, and explain the minimum-length rule they impose
Explain that array and tuple types are covariant in their member types, so `S[]` is a subtype of `T[]` when `S` is a subtype of `T`
Explain that a list's inherent type is enforced at runtime, so storing a value that does not belong to the member type (e.g. through a `(int|string)[]` view of an `int[]`) panics
Use spread members `...expr` in list constructors to splice the members of another list, and know the spread expression must have a list static type

Explain how a list constructor takes its inherent type from the contextually expected type (including choosing the single matching list type in a union), and infers a tuple type from the members' broad types when there is no expected type

Rely on filler values so a list constructor may give only the first k members of a fixed-length array (e.g. `int[5] a = [1, 2];`), and know this is a compile error when the member type has no filler value
Explain that reading `arr[i]` with `i < 0` or `i >= arr.length()` panics, and guard indexes against the length

Explain that assigning to `arr[k]` with `k` greater than the length fills the gap using filler values, and panics if filling fails, for example on a fixed-length array or a member type with no filler value
Iterate over the members of an array or tuple in order with `foreach`, where the iteration value type of `T[]` is `T`
Write byte array literals with `base16 `...`` and `base64 `...``, which have static type `byte[N]` (or a readonly singleton type when the expected type is readonly or inside a const-expr)
Use `lang.array` functions through method-call syntax, such as `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `slice`, `remove`, `indexOf`, `reverse`, `sort`, `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `forEach` and `enumerate`

nodes.notes: Spec 5.4.1.1 says `v[i][j]` is valid iff 0 ≤ i ≤ M and 0 ≤ j ≤ N; this reads as an off-by-one in the spec text (should be < M, < N). Items follow the member-access semantics in 6.14 (index must be < length).

nodes.title: Assignment
nodes.summary: Assignment and compound assignment statements, with the lvalue model that defines how stores, removals, reads and filling-reads work on variables, object fields and structure members.

must_cover.text: Write assignments `x = expr;`, `obj.f = expr;`, `m["k"] = expr;` and `arr[i] = expr;`, where the left side type provides the contextually expected type for the right side
Explain that an lvalue refers to a variable, a named object field or a structure member with an out-of-line key (list index or mapping key), and never to a table member
Explain that an assignment statement evaluates the right-hand side before evaluating the left-hand lvexpr
Explain that assigning `()` to an optional mapping member whose type excludes nil (e.g. `r.f = ();` for `int f?`) removes the member, and removing an absent member has no effect

Explain why stores into structure members are checked at runtime and panic when they would violate the inherent type, add a key a closed record or fixed-length list disallows, or mutate an immutable value
Explain that removing a member panics when the inherent type requires that key or the mapping is immutable
Explain chained assignment such as `m["a"]["b"] = 1;`, where a missing intermediate member is created by a filling-read using filler values, and the store panics if no filler value can be made
Explain that `lv.f = v` on a mapping requires `f` to be an individual field of the type (in every union member) and `lv` not to be potentially uninitialized, though it may be potentially undefined
Explain that `lv[k] = v` needs a `string` key for mappings and an `int` key for lists

Use compound assignment operators `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=` and `>>>=`, where `x op= e` must be valid for the non-nil-lifted operator and its result must be a subtype of the type of `x`
Explain that a compound assignment target must not be potentially uninitialized or potentially undefined (unless it is a list member), and that it panics at runtime if the list member is undefined
Explain that assigning to a module variable declared `isolated` is allowed only inside a `lock` statement

out_of_scope: Variable declarations, final and definite assignment (concept.variables)
nodes.notes: 7.14.1 member-access-lvexpr evaluation says 'evaluate expression ... then evaluate lvexpr' (key before container), whereas 6.14 member-access-expr evaluates container first; the lvalue text also says 'member of c' where it means v (typo).

nodes.title: Basic types
nodes.summary: How Ballerina partitions values into basic types, describes them with structural type descriptors and semantic subtyping, and the simple nil and boolean types.

must_cover.text: Classify values into the four kinds of basic type: simple (nil, boolean, int, float, decimal, tagged data), sequence (string, xml), structured (list, mapping, table) and behavioral (error, function, future, object, typedesc, handle, stream)
Explain that every value belongs to exactly one basic type, so for example the empty string, the empty xml value and nil are distinct values

Explain storage identity, that structured and behavioral values have it while simple values do not, so variables and members hold references to such values and mutation through one reference is visible through all of them

Explain that a type denotes a set of shapes and that subtyping is semantic, so S is a subtype of T exactly when every shape in S is in T, with no explicit declaration of compatibility (structural typing)
Define plain data as simple values, sequence values and structured values containing no behavioral values at any depth, and know that plain data (even cyclic) can be compared for equality

Name the type descriptor for each basic type (`()`, `boolean`, `int`, `float`, `decimal`, `string`, `xml`, array, tuple, `map`, record, `table`, `error`, `function`, `future`, `object`, `typedesc`, `handle`, `stream`) and the other descriptors (singleton, `readonly`, `any`, `never`, optional, union, intersection, `distinct`, `anydata`, `json`, `byte`)

Apply type-descriptor precedence: `distinct T` binds tightest, then `T[]` and `T?`, then `T1 & T2`, then `T1 | T2` (both left-associative), then `function(args) returns T` (right-associative), and use `( T )` to group
Use the nil value `()` to represent absence of a value, know `null` is an alternative spelling meant only for JSON-related contexts, and that nil is the only basic type with a single value
Use the `boolean` type with the literals `true` and `false`
Explain that all simple basic types are inherently immutable and that a simple type descriptor contains every value of its basic type
Define named types with `type Name T;` (optionally `public`) and refer to them by a type reference, unqualified or as `prefix:Name` for a type defined in another module
Explain that a value has exactly one basic type yet can belong to arbitrarily many types, because type descriptors such as unions and singletons describe overlapping subsets of the universe of values

out_of_scope: Numeric types int, float, decimal and byte (concept.numeric_types)
Union, optional, singleton, any, never and intersection descriptors in detail (concept.union_intersection_types)
Read-only bit and the readonly type (concept.mutability_readonly)

edges.note: type names and literals are built from lexical tokens
each basic type has a corresponding lang library module

nodes.notes: The 5.1.4 table lists `distinct` with an empty value-set description; items do not attempt to define it beyond 5.6.6.

nodes.title: Binding patterns
nodes.summary: Capture, wildcard, list, mapping and error binding patterns, typed binding patterns with `var`, and destructuring assignment.

must_cover.text: Use a capture binding pattern `x` to bind any value and the wildcard `_`, and know that `_` matches only values whose basic type is not error
Destructure lists with `[a, b]` and `[first, ...rest]`, where the pattern matches when it has no more members than the list and `rest` gets a new list of the remaining members
Destructure mappings with `{name: n, age}` (the shorthand `age` means `age: age`) and `{id, ...others}`, where `others` gets a new mapping of the unmatched fields
Explain that a field binding pattern binds `()` for an absent field only when the field is known at compile time to be optional and unable to hold nil
Destructure errors with `error(msg, cause, code = c, ...rest)` and `error MyError(msg)`, matching the message, the optional cause, named detail fields and the remaining detail fields
Explain that all variables in one binding pattern must be distinct, so `[x, x]` is not allowed
Write typed binding patterns with an explicit type or `var`, e.g. `var [x, y] = point;`, where `var` infers the type from the initializer
Distinguish single use of a typed binding pattern (followed by `=`, or after `on fail`) from iterative use (followed by `in`), where `var` infers the iteration value type
Explain the compile error when `var x = expr;` infers a type that may include an error and `x` is never used
Explain that a typed binding pattern whose type descriptor is `never` is an error
Explain that a binding pattern in a typed binding pattern must be consistent with the type and irrefutable, so the compiler guarantees the match cannot fail at runtime
Derive the type a binding pattern implies: a tuple type for a list pattern, a record type for a mapping pattern, an error type for an error pattern and `any` for `_`
Assign to existing variables with destructuring assignment such as `[a, b] = [b, a];` or `{x, y} = p;`, where the right side must be a subtype of the type the pattern implies
Explain that a destructuring assignment pattern must not refer to a module variable declared `isolated`
Use a declaration such as `Z _ = v;` in the final else branch to make the compiler check that `v` has been narrowed to `Z`, so adding a new member to the union causes a compile error

out_of_scope: Local and module variable declarations in general (concept.variables)
Binding patterns in query from/join/let clauses (concept.query_expressions)
nodes.notes: Error binding pattern grammar: `error [error-type-reference] ( [message-bp [, cause-bp]] [, named-arg-bp ...] [, ...rest] )`.

nodes.title: Classes
nodes.summary: Module-level class definitions that describe an object type and how to construct it, the init method rules and the new expression.

must_cover.text: Define classes such as `class Person { string name; function init(string name) { self.name = name; } }`, optionally `public`, containing fields, methods, remote and resource methods and object type inclusions
Apply the class qualifiers `distinct`, `readonly`, `isolated`, `client` and `service` to a class definition, knowing each keyword may appear at most once
Use `private` fields and methods, visible only within the class's method definitions, and know that a class with private members has no other object types as subtypes
Create instances with `new Person("Ann")`, which allocates the object and passes the argument list to the class's `init` method, with a compile error if the arguments do not match `init`'s signature
Use implicit `new` or `new(args)` when the applicable contextually expected type is a class or stream type, e.g. `Person p = new("Ann");`
Declare `init` with return type `error?` and explain that `new T(...)` then has static type `T|E` and evaluates to the error value instead of the object when `init` returns an error

Follow the `init` method rules: its return type must be a subtype of `error?` that contains `()`, it cannot be `private`, it is not part of the object's shape, and it can be called explicitly only as `self.init(...)`

Explain that within `init` the compiler tracks potentially uninitialized fields, and it is a compile error to read such a field, or to return nil or use `self` other than to access or modify a field while any field is potentially uninitialized
Know that a class's `init` method may declare parameters, whereas an `init` method in an object constructor must have an empty parameter list
Explain that a missing `init` method is equivalent to an isolated `init` with no parameters and an empty body

Explain that if a field initializer completes with a check-fail, `init` returns that error before its body runs (so `init`'s return type must allow it), and that without an `init` method a `check` in a field initializer is a compile error
Describe how an object of a class is initialized: allocate storage, run each field initializer, attach the methods from the class's method definitions, then call `init` if there is one

Include an object type in a class with `*T;`, which requires the class to define every method declared in `T` with the same visibility (and to be in `T`'s module if `T` has module-level members); including a class copies only its type, not its method bodies or field initializers

Define a `readonly class` whose objects have the read-only bit set, where each field's effective type is its declared type intersected with `readonly` and only read-only objects belong to the class's type
Define a `distinct class` whose primary type-id comes from that `distinct` occurrence, with the type-ids of included object types as secondary type-ids

Define an `isolated class`, whose objects have the isolated bit set and whose fields and methods follow the rules of an explicitly isolated object constructor (non-isolated fields must be `private` and initializers must be isolated expressions)

out_of_scope: Object type descriptors and object constructors (concept.objects)
Detailed isolated-object rules for self and lock (concept.isolation, concept.lock_statement)
nodes.notes: 6.8.1.5 says it is a compile error for init to 'access a field at a point where it is potentially initialized'; this is a typo for 'potentially uninitialized'. 6.8.2 says 'An explicit-type-expr specifying a class-descriptor T has static type T' (should be explicit-new-expr).

nodes.title: Client objects
nodes.summary: Network interaction objects for outbound calls, their remote methods and resources, and the remote method call and resource access actions used to invoke them.

must_cover.text: Distinguish client objects (network interaction originated by the program) from service objects (interaction originated by the remote system), knowing an object can be one, the other or neither, but not both
Declare client object types and classes with the `client` qualifier, e.g. `client class Api { ... }`, knowing only client objects belong to an object type that has the `client` qualifier

Declare remote methods with `remote function send(string msg) returns error?`, allowed only in client or service objects and kept in a symbol space separate from fields and ordinary methods, so a remote method may share a name with a non-remote method

Explain that an object constructor must specify `client` if it defines a remote method, and that remote and resource method definitions are allowed only when a network qualifier (`client` or `service`) is present
Call a client's remote method with the action `clientObj->send("hi")`, knowing a remote method cannot be called with `.` method-call syntax and `->` has the same precedence as `.`
Know that the return type of a client object's remote method must not be `never`

Explain that remote method calls and resource accesses are actions: they cannot be nested inside expressions and occur only as part of statements or inside other actions such as `check`, `trap` or a type cast

Access a client's resources with the resource access action, e.g. `check c->/users/[id].get()` or `c->/users.post(user)`, where an omitted method name defaults to `get` and omitted parentheses default to an empty argument list

Use computed path segments `[expr]` and a rest segment `[...segments]` in a resource access path, and `c->/` for the empty path; evaluation builds a list of path values from names, computed values and the members of the rest list

Explain that the client's static type must contain a resource with the given method name for every path the access could construct, and that arguments and the result are typed using the intersection of the function types of the matching resource methods
Explain that a local variable of client object type is shown as a lifeline in the function's sequence diagram, and a remote method call as a horizontal arrow from the worker to that lifeline

out_of_scope: Resource method declarations and resource paths (concept.resource_methods)
Protocol-specific clients such as HTTP, which belong to the standard library
nodes.notes: 5.5.3.1 says 'A object-network-qual is not allowed in conjunction with public', but object-type-quals has no public; the intended restriction is unclear, so no item states it.

nodes.title: Comparison
nodes.summary: Deep equality (==), exact equality (===), the DeepEquals operation, ordered types and the Compare operations behind relational operators and sorting.

must_cover.text: Use `==` and `!=` for deep equality of values, knowing at least one operand must have a static type that is a subtype of `anydata`
Use `===` and `!==` for exact equality, which compares storage identity for structured and behavioral values and identical values for simple values
Explain that all four equality operators give a compile error when the intersection of the operands' static types is empty

Explain that DeepEquals compares the primary aspect of shapes, ignoring read-only bits, terminates on cyclic values, is false for values of different basic types, and that `x.clone() == x` always holds for anydata x
Explain float equality edge cases, that `==` treats `0.0` and `-0.0` as equal while `===` does not, and both treat NaN as equal to NaN, unlike IEEE comparison
Explain that `==` on decimals ignores precision while `===` does not, so `1.0d == 1.00d` is true but `1.0d === 1.00d` is false

Explain exact equality for strings and xml, where sequences are exactly equal if they have the same length and corresponding constituents are exactly equal (singletons compare storage identity when they have it)
Use `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, which require both operands to belong to a common ordered type and have static type boolean
Identify ordered types, namely nil, boolean (false < true), int, float, decimal, string (by Unicode code point), optional versions `T?` of ordered types, and lists whose member types are ordered
Explain that comparing NaN or comparing nil with a non-nil value is unordered, so every relational operator returns false (e.g. `float:NaN < 1.0` and `float:NaN >= 1.0` are both false)
Explain lexicographic comparison of lists, where `[]` is less than any non-empty list and the first unequal member pair decides
Explain that sorting (array `sort` and query `order by`) uses CompareA/CompareD so that nil and NaN always sort last, with NaN before nil, in both ascending and descending order
Explain that ordering comparisons on decimals ignore precision and that `-0.0` and `+0.0` compare equal for floats

nodes.notes: 6.29 says === on simple types requires 'identical values within the possible of values allowed for T' (garbled phrase). 5.8.6 lists nil, boolean, int, string as 'these three types' though four are named.

nodes.title: Configurable variables
nodes.summary: Module-level variables declared `configurable` whose values can be supplied by a configuration when the program is run.

must_cover.text: Declare a configurable module variable such as `configurable int port = 8080;`, whose initializer is used only when no value is supplied; if a value is supplied when the program is run, the initializer expression is not evaluated
Use `configurable string password = ?;` to require that the configuration supply a value, knowing a `?` initializer is allowed only with `configurable`
Explain that a configurable declaration must use an explicit type descriptor rather than `var`, its binding pattern must be just a variable name, and the type must be a subtype of `anydata`
Explain that a configurable variable is implicitly final and cannot be assigned outside its declaration, and that its static type is the declared type intersected with `readonly`
Recognize that `configurable` is used on its own in the module variable qualifiers: it cannot be combined with `final` or `isolated`
Reference configurable variables from `isolated` functions, which is always allowed because a configurable variable is final and its type is a subtype of `readonly`

Explain that a configuration maps configurable variable names to values of type `anydata & readonly`, and that before any module is initialized the initialization phase checks that every required configurable variable has a value of the correct type, terminating unsuccessfully otherwise

out_of_scope: Configuration file formats and command-line overrides (platform-defined, e.g. Config.toml)
nodes.notes: 8.7 says that with `var` the precise type is used 'if the module-var-decl includes final or configurable', yet a configurable declaration may not use `var`; the configurable half of that sentence appears vacuous. The format in which the configuration is supplied is not defined by the spec.

nodes.title: Constants and enums
nodes.summary: Compile-time constants declared with const, the constant expressions that initialize them, and enum declarations as unions of string constants.

must_cover.text: Declare module constants with `const MAX = 10;` or `public const string GREETING = "hi";`, naming immutable values known at compile time

Explain that a constant's type is the intersection of `readonly` and the singleton type of its value, so an explicit type descriptor only supplies the contextually expected type and an upper bound; it must be a subtype of `anydata` and not `never`, and the const-expr's static type must be a subtype of it
Use constants where compile-time values are required: as singleton types in type descriptors (e.g. `type Mode READ|WRITE;`), as array lengths such as `int[N]`, and in match patterns

Write constant expressions from literals, template expressions, list/mapping/table constructors, references to other constants, type casts, `is` tests, and unary, arithmetic, relational, equality, logical and conditional operators, where every nested expression must itself be a const-expr
Know that a constant reference inside a const-expr must refer to a constant defined with a module `const` declaration

Explain that a const-expr is evaluated at compile time, that constructors within it build values with the read-only bit set so the result is always immutable, and that a const-expr cannot construct an error value
Declare structured constants such as `const map<int> LIMITS = {low: 1, high: 9};` or `const int[] PRIMES = [2, 3, 5];`, whose values are immutable

Distinguish `simple-const-expr` (nil, boolean, optionally signed numeric literals, string literals and constant references), which is used for singleton types, const match patterns and xmlns namespace URIs, from a full const-expr

Declare enums such as `enum Color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }`, where each member becomes a string constant whose value defaults to its own name and the enum name becomes a type that is the union of the member constants
Give enum members explicit values such as `RED = "red"`, knowing the const-expr must evaluate to a string

Explain that `public enum Color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }` is exactly equivalent to `public const RED = "RED";` (and so on) plus `public type Color RED|GREEN|BLUE;`, so a public enum makes both the type and the constants public

out_of_scope: Singleton and union types in general (concept.union_intersection_types)
nodes.notes: Section 6.4 lists the syntactic forms of const-expr; the spec does not enumerate which operators are allowed inside nil-lifted-expr beyond the grammar, so items follow the grammar list.

nodes.title: Control flow
nodes.summary: How statements and statement blocks execute and complete, including if/else, do, return, call, action and checking statements, and the distinction between actions and expressions.

must_cover.text: Write `if cond { ... } else if cond { ... } else { ... }` statements whose conditions have static type boolean, executing the first block whose condition is true or the `else` block if none is
Use a `do { ... }` statement to execute a statement block as a single compound statement (commonly so that an `on fail` clause can be attached)
Use `return expr;` to terminate the current worker normally with a value, and know that `return;` and falling off the end of a body are equivalent to `return ();`
Explain that a statement block `{ ... }` runs its statements in order and that as soon as one statement does not complete normally none of the following statements run

Distinguish the three ways a statement can complete: normally, by terminating the current worker (return, panic, unhandled fail), or by transferring control within the worker (break, continue, fail to an on fail clause)
Explain that when an expression in a statement completes abruptly, a check-fail behaves like a `fail` statement with that error value and a panic terminates the worker like a `panic` statement

Explain that any unreachable statement other than `panic` is a compile-time error (e.g. code after `return`), and that reachability analysis assumes a condition can be true or false unless its static type (such as singleton `true`) rules it out
Use a function or method call as a statement only when its static type is `()` or `never`; to discard a non-nil result, use a destructuring assignment to the wildcard such as `_ = f();`
Write an action (such as a remote method call `c->m();`, a send or a `wait`) as a statement only when its static type is nil
Write `check f();` or `checkpanic f();` as a checking statement when the checked call's non-error result type is `()`

Distinguish actions (start, wait, send, receive, flush, `->` remote method calls, `->/` resource access, query actions, commit) from expressions, and know an action cannot be nested inside an expression but may appear in a statement or inside `check`, `trap`, a type cast or another action
Know that the `->` operator of a client remote method call action has the same precedence as `.` in a method call expression

out_of_scope: fail, on fail, panic and trap semantics (concept.error_handling)
nodes.notes: 7.16 says that if a call-stmt's static type is `never`, then 'it is possible for the call-stmt to complete normally'; this looks like a typo for 'not possible' and was not turned into an item.

nodes.title: Documentation
nodes.summary: Documentation strings written as lines starting with

must_cover.text: Write documentation strings as one or more lines that each start with `#` (optionally preceded by spaces or tabs) placed before module-level constructs and method declarations, knowing a documentation string is recognized only at the start of a line
Explain that a single space after `#` is not part of the content, and that the concatenated content is parsed as Ballerina Flavored Markdown, which is GitHub Flavored Markdown with extra conventions
Put information useful to users of a module in documentation strings, and information not useful for that purpose in comments
Document every parameter of a function or method, and its return value if it is not nil, as Markdown list items `+ name - description` and `+ return - description`
Document an object with a list of its fields instead of parameters, leaving out private fields

Refer to Ballerina names in documentation by putting `type`, `service`, `variable`, `var`, `annotation`, `module`, `function` or `parameter` before a backticked identifier, or by writing a backticked call form such as `x()`, `m:x()`, `T.y()` or `m:T.y()`

Explain how documentation references resolve: a `parameter` reference names a parameter of the documented function, an unqualified name must be a public name of the right kind in the module, and a qualified `M:X` requires `M` to be imported and `X` to be public in `M`
Know that Ballerina Flavored Markdown is also used for a separate per-module documentation file, conventionally called `Module.md`
Use a heading with the content `Deprecated` in a documentation string to document that the name it is attached to is deprecated, a platform-defined convention

out_of_scope: Comments (`//`), which are lexical white space (concept.lexical_structure)
API documentation generation tools, which are platform features

nodes.title: Error handling
nodes.summary: Propagating, handling and converting errors with check and checkpanic, fail and on fail clauses, panic and trap, and how failure differs from panic.

must_cover.text: Use `check expr` to propagate errors: if `expr` evaluates to an error the evaluation completes with a check-fail carrying that error, otherwise the result has the static type T obtained by removing the error part E from `T|E`
Use `checkpanic expr` to turn an unexpected error into a panic, removing the error part from the static type in the same way as `check`
Know that a type cast such as `<int>f()` cannot cast away an error (a compile-time error when the operand may be an error and the target type excludes error), so use `check` or `checkpanic` instead

Explain that evaluating an expression can complete abruptly with a check-fail or a panic, each carrying an error value, and that an enclosing expression then completes abruptly in the same way unless stated otherwise

Distinguish failure (from `check` or `fail`, whose error types are known at compile time and which transfers control to the nearest failure-handling statement) from panic (abnormal termination of the worker, whose error type is not known at compile time)

Know that a failure with no enclosing failure-handling statement (on fail, retry, transaction, retry transaction) terminates the current worker normally with the error as its return value, so `check` in a function needs an error type in its return type
Use `fail expr;`, where `expr` is a subtype of error, to fail explicitly to the nearest failure handler or to return the error from the worker

Attach `on fail error e { ... }` (or `on fail var e`, or no binding) to a `do`, `while`, `foreach`, `match`, `lock`, `retry`, `transaction` or `retry transaction` statement to handle failures from `check` and `fail` inside it (on fail for retry and transaction statements is new in 2024R1)

Know that the on fail binding must be guaranteed to match the union of error types from the enclosed check expressions and fail statements, that `var` infers this type, and that `on fail var e` with `e` never used is a compile-time error

Know that when the statement carrying `on fail` is itself a failure-handling statement (retry or transaction), only that statement's own failure reaches the clause, while failures inside it are first handled by that statement
Attach `on fail` to a named worker declaration, as in `worker w { ... } on fail error e { ... }`, which is equivalent to wrapping the worker body in `do { ... } on fail` (new in 2024R1)
Use `panic expr;` with an error-typed expression to terminate the current worker abnormally with that error as its termination value
Use `trap expr` to stop a panic and obtain its error value, giving static type `T|error` (T may be `never`)

Recognize runtime panics the spec defines: int overflow and division by zero, out-of-range list or string index, failed type casts, impermissible stores into structured values, `checkpanic` on an error, and langlib functions documented to panic

Know that `check` on a lax json expression whose contextually expected type is a simple type, as in `int n = check j.count;`, is treated as `check value:ensureType(...)`, so a type mismatch becomes a check-fail instead of a compile error

out_of_scope: Error values and the error constructor (concept.errors)
Lax typing of json in general (concept.json_anydata)
nodes.notes: 7.23 says a failure without a handler 'terminates the current worker normally' with the error as return value; the item about needing an error in the return type is a consequence of the typing rules, not a separate sentence of the spec.

nodes.title: Errors
nodes.summary: The error basic type (message, cause, detail and stack trace), error<T> and distinct error types, the error constructor, and the lang.error functions for inspecting errors.

must_cover.text: Explain the four parts of an error value: a message string, an optional cause (another error or nil), an immutable detail mapping, and a stack trace, which is not part of the error's shape
Explain that errors form a separate, inherently immutable basic type excluded from `any`, so fallible functions return `T|error` and `any|error` covers every value
Know that a list or mapping containing error members still belongs to `any`, because only values whose basic type is error are excluded
Construct errors with `error("message")`, `error("message", cause)` and detail fields as named arguments, as in `error("not found", code = 404)`

Use `error<T>`, where T is a detail record type (a subtype of `map<value:Cloneable>`, see `error:Detail`), to constrain the detail, and define named error types such as `type NotFound error<record {| int code; |}>;`

Construct a named error type with `error NotFound("msg", code = 1)` or from a contextually expected error type, where named arguments must be fields of the detail record and defaults are filled in from it
Know that named-argument values must be subtypes of `value:Cloneable` and that the detail mapping is built immutable by applying ImmutableClone, so `e.detail()` returns a `readonly` value

Define distinct error types such as `type IoError distinct error;` and intersections such as `IoError & TimeoutError`, so that error values carry type-ids, and know the error constructor's expected type must be definite
Know that an error's stack trace captures the execution stack where the error constructor was evaluated, and read it with `e.stackTrace()` as an array of `error:StackFrame`
Inspect errors with the lang.error functions `e.message()`, `e.cause()`, `e.detail()`, `e.toString()` and `e.toBalString()`
Recognize the built-in distinct error types `error:NoMessage` (a receive action whose message was never sent) and `error:Retriable` (errors that `error:DefaultRetryManager` will retry)

out_of_scope: check, checkpanic, trap, fail, on fail and panic (concept.error_handling)
Error binding and match patterns (concept.binding_patterns, concept.match_statement)
Type-ids and distinct types in general (concept.type_ids_distinct)

nodes.title: Expressions
nodes.summary: How expressions are evaluated (normal and abrupt completion), operator precedence, and how static types are computed using contextually expected types, precise and broad types, and singleton typing.

must_cover.text: Apply expression precedence from highest to lowest: `m:x`, `x.k`, `x.@a`, `f(x)`, `x.f(y)`, `x[y]`, `new T(x)`; then unary `+ - ~ !`, `<T> x`, `typeof`, `check`, `checkpanic`; `* / %`; `+ -`; shifts; ranges `...`/`..<`; relational and `is`/`!is`; equality; `&`; `^`; `|`; `&&`; `||`; `?:`; `? :`; and finally `=>`, `let`, query and `trap`

Know that binary arithmetic, shift, equality, bitwise and logical operators are left-associative, range and relational operators are non-associative, and `?:`, `? :`, lambdas, `let`, queries and `trap` are right-associative

Distinguish the two kinds of abrupt completion, check-fail and panic, both carrying an error value, and know that abrupt completion of a subexpression makes the enclosing expression complete abruptly in the same way unless stated otherwise

Explain that if an expression completes normally its value belongs to the expression's compile-time static type, that a (possibly empty) error type is also computed for check-fail, and that no type is computed for panics
Explain that it is a compile error for an expression to have static type `never` except where the spec explicitly allows it (such as calls to functions returning `never`)
Explain the contextually expected type, for example that the declared type of a variable is the expected type of its initializer, and that constructors use it to decide what type of value to build

Explain how the applicable contextually expected type is obtained by normalizing the expected type to a union of single-basic-type members and keeping only those of the constructor's basic type, with a compile error if none remain
Explain that when a variable is declared with `var` there is no contextually expected type for its initializer, which is different from an expected type that allows all values

Distinguish an expression's precise and broad static types, for example the literal `"X"` has precise type the singleton `"X"` and broad type `string`, and the broad type is used to infer non-final `var` variables and member types of inferred inherent types
Apply the usual singleton typing rules, so a compound expression whose operands all have singleton types gets a singleton static type computed at compile time (e.g. `1 + 2` has static type `3`)

edges.note: numeric literal typing uses the contextually expected type

nodes.notes: 6.2 states that the detailed static typing rules are not yet completely specified in 2024R1; items only cover what is stated.

nodes.title: External functions
nodes.summary: Functions whose implementation lives outside the Ballerina module, and the handle type that refers to externally managed storage.

must_cover.text: Declare a function whose implementation is not provided in the Ballerina source module with an external body, e.g. `function now() returns int = external;`, optionally with annotations before `external`
Explain that a function whose signature is dependently typed (its return type references a `typedesc` parameter) must have an external function body
Use the `handle` type for references to storage managed outside the Ballerina program, knowing a new handle value can only be created by a function with an external body
Explain that handle values are inherently immutable and that a value belongs to `handle` exactly when its basic type is handle

Explain that an `isolated` function with an external body must, in its external implementation, access only mutable state reachable from its parameters and behave correctly when called concurrently on multiple strands
Explain that a function with an external body may yield its strand, and should do so only when it makes a blocking system call or calls a Ballerina function that yields
Annotate an external function body using an annotation declared with the source-only `external` attachment point (`on source external`)

out_of_scope: Platform-specific interop mechanisms (e.g. Java interop), which the spec does not define

nodes.title: Member access
nodes.summary: The `x.f`, `x?.f` and `x[k]` expressions for reading object fields, mapping members, list, string and xml constituents, including their static types, nil results and panics.

must_cover.text: Read a record field with `r.name`, and explain that for a non-lax type the field must be a required key of a mapping type, giving static type the field type
Explain that `r.f` on a non-lax record where `f` is an optional field whose type excludes nil is treated as `r?.f` and so can evaluate to `()`
Use `x?.f` to read a possibly absent field, returning `()` when `x` is `()` or has no field `f`, with static type including `()` in those cases
Explain that for a non-lax type, `x?.f` requires the static type to be a subtype of `()` or mapping and the type descriptor to declare `f` as an individual field (in at least one union member)

Access object fields with `obj.f`, and explain that `obj.m` naming a method yields a new function value with `self` bound to `obj`, which is isolated only if both the object and the method are isolated

Explain that on lax types such as `json`, `j.a` and `j?.a` have static type including `error`, returning an error when the value is not a mapping or (for `.`) the key is missing, and passing an error operand through unchanged
Explain the key type rules for `c[k]`: `int` for lists, strings and xml, the key type `K` for `table<R> key<K>`, and `string` for mappings (where the container may also be `()`)
Index lists and strings with `c[i]`, knowing that `i < 0` or `i >= length` panics and that indexing a string gives a `string:Char`
Index xml values with `x[i]`, which panics for a negative index but returns the empty xml value when `i` is beyond the length, with static type `M|E` for `xml<M>`
Read mapping members with `m["key"]`, which returns `()` when the key is absent or `m` is `()`, so the static type is `T?` for a map or an optional record field
Explain that the multi-key form `c[k1, k2]` is allowed only when the container is a table
Explain that a member access evaluates the container expression before the key expression

out_of_scope: XML attribute access with `.` and `?.` on xml values (concept.xml_navigation)
Assignment through field and member access (concept.assignment)
nodes.notes: 6.10 says a field-access-expr on an xml static type is interpreted as an xml-required-attribute-access-expr; that case lives in concept.xml_navigation.

nodes.title: Filler values
nodes.summary: The FillMember abstract operation and the filler value defined for each type descriptor, which let lists and mappings be filled in automatically.

must_cover.text: Explain FillMember(s, k), which adds a member with key k to a structured value only if its inherent type allows that key and a filler value exists for the required member type, and otherwise fails
Name the filler values of simple types: `()` for nil, `false` for boolean, `0` for int, byte and built-in int subtypes, `+0.0f` for float, `+0d` for decimal and `""` for string

Explain that arrays and tuples have filler `[]` and maps and records have filler `{}` only when that is a valid constructor for the type (so a record with required fields has no filler), and tables fill with an empty table

Name the remaining fillers, namely an empty stream for streams, `xml``` for xml and for `xml:Text` (but not other xml built-in subtypes), `re``` for `regexp:RegExp`, and the single value for a singleton type
Explain that an object type has filler `new T()` only when T is a class whose `init` method allows no arguments and cannot return an error

Explain union fillers: `()` when nil is a member (so `T?`, `any`, `anydata` and `json` fill with `()`), or the basic type's filler when all members share one basic type and that filler belongs to the union; `readonly & T` uses T's filler constructed read-only if it belongs
Use filler values to give fewer members than a fixed length in a list constructor, e.g. `int[3] a = [1];` yields `[1, 0, 0]`, which is a compile error when the member type has no filler
Explain that storing to index k beyond a list's length fills indices in between with FillMember, and panics if filling fails, for example on a fixed-length array
Explain the filling-read used by chained assignments such as `m["a"]["b"] = 1;`, which creates a missing intermediate member with FillMember and panics if no filler exists

nodes.notes: Filling-read is described for lvalues with a structured static type; the example `m["a"]["b"] = 1` assumes the member type of m has a `{}` filler (e.g. map<map<int>>).

nodes.title: Function values
nodes.summary: Functions as first-class values described by function type descriptors, created with anonymous function expressions and called dynamically.

must_cover.text: Write function type descriptors such as `function (int, string) returns boolean` and store, pass and return function values like any other value
Use the bare `function` type, to which every function value belongs, and `isolated function`, to which exactly the isolated function values belong
Explain that function types are covariant in their return type and contravariant in their parameter list type, and that parameter names and default values do not affect a function's shape or typing
Explain that a function type with an `isolated` qualifier admits only function values whose isolated bit is set, while a type without it ignores the isolated bit

Explain that a function value with the transactional bit set can only be called in a transactional scope, so a function type without `transactional` is a subtype of the same type with `transactional`, the opposite direction to `isolated`
Write explicit anonymous functions such as `function (int x) returns int { return x + 1; }` or `function (int x) returns int => x + 1`

Write inferred anonymous functions such as `x => x * 2` or `(a, b) => a + b` in contexts that expect a function type, where the parameter types and whether the function is `isolated` are inferred from the expected type

Explain that an inferred anonymous function's return type is the static type of its body expression, which gets the expected function type's return type as its contextually expected type, and that it is inferred `transactional` if the body calls transactional functions
Explain that an anonymous function captures outer local variables by reference: the closure refers to the same storage as the original variable, not a copy
Call a function value held in a variable or parameter with ordinary call syntax `f(1)`, and call an object field of function type with method-call syntax `obj.handler(1)`

Obtain a method as a function value with field access `obj.method` (without calling it), producing a function that calls the method with `self` bound to `obj`, whose isolated bit is set only if both the object and the method are isolated
Call a function dynamically with `function:call(func, ...args)` from lang.function, which returns `any|error` and panics if the arguments are not of the types the function requires

Explain that the closures computing default parameter values are part of a function's type descriptor, created when it is resolved and called by the caller, and that with an `isolated` function type a default expression must meet the isolated-function requirements

out_of_scope: Isolation rules for captured variables in isolated functions (concept.isolation)

nodes.title: Functions
nodes.summary: Defining functions with required, defaultable, included-record and rest parameters, returning values, and calling them with positional, named and spread arguments.

must_cover.text: Define module-level functions such as `function add(int a, int b) returns int { return a + b; }`, optionally qualified with `public`, `isolated` and/or `transactional`
Explain that a function always returns exactly one value: an omitted return type means `returns ()`, and `return;` or falling off the end of the body returns `()`
Declare `returns never` for a function that never returns normally, and know a call to it has static type `never`
Write expression-bodied functions such as `function square(int x) returns int => x * x;`, which is short for a body `{ return x * x; }`
Declare required parameters `T name` and supply them as positional arguments in declaration order, knowing omitting an argument for a required parameter is a compile error
Explain that parameters are initialized from the argument list before the body runs and are implicitly final: they can be read but not assigned

Declare defaultable parameters such as `int retries = 3`, whose default expression may refer to earlier parameters and is evaluated by the caller each time the argument is omitted, in parameter declaration order
Declare a rest parameter `string... names`, which receives the remaining arguments as a newly created list whose inherent type is `string[]`

Call functions with named arguments after positional ones, e.g. `connect("host", port = 8080)`, knowing every argument name must be distinct and it is an error to supply the same parameter both positionally and by name

Pass a list's members as positional arguments with a spread rest argument `f(...values)`, or a mapping's fields as named arguments with `f(...options)`, where the spread's static type must make the equivalent arguments valid

Declare included record parameters such as `*Options opts` so callers can pass the record's fields as named arguments (e.g. `send(msg, timeout = 5)`), with unspecified fields defaulted from the record type, and know field names must be distinct from each other and from parameter names
Explain that if an argument is given for an included record parameter itself, its fields cannot also be passed as named arguments, and that a non-optional field without a default must be supplied

Explain that a named argument can match a rest descriptor of an included record parameter only when that record type declares every other parameter name and included field name as an optional `never` field, has no other individual fields, and no other included record parameter has a rest descriptor

Explain that argument expressions are evaluated in the order they occur, with contextually expected types taken from the parameter types, and that the declared type of the referenced function variable, not the runtime function value, is used to build the argument list
Explain that a function call completes abruptly with a panic if the called function terminates abnormally, and that the call's static type is the function's return type, which may be `never`
Know that a required or defaultable parameter's type must not be `never`, and that parameter names may be omitted only in a function type descriptor's signature

Explain dependently-typed signatures such as `function convert(json v, typedesc<anydata> t = <>) returns t|error`, where the `<>` default makes the caller infer the typedesc argument from the call's contextually expected type; `<>` is allowed for at most one parameter and only if that parameter is referenced in the return type

out_of_scope: Function types, function values and anonymous functions (concept.function_values)
Method calls on objects and langlib method-call dispatch (concept.objects, concept.langlib_conventions)
nodes.notes: 5.5.2 states dependently-typed functions can be declared and used but Ballerina does not yet provide a mechanism to define them (so in practice they are external/langlib functions such as value:cloneWithType).

nodes.title: Futures and wait
nodes.summary: Running calls asynchronously with start, future types, waiting for one, several or the first of many strands, and cancelling futures.

must_cover.text: Use `start f(args)` (or a method call, remote method call or resource access) to run a call on a new strand and immediately get a `future<T>`, with the arguments evaluated on the current strand
Explain future types: `future<T>` refers to a strand that will return a T, and `future` without a type parameter covers every future value

Know that a start whose call is isolated (an isolated callee with isolated argument expressions, the receiver object counting as an argument) is allowed in isolated functions and may run on a separate thread
Use `wait f` to wait for a strand to terminate and get its termination value

Explain wait result types: waiting on a named worker's name has eventual type T and cannot fail, while waiting on any other `future<T>` gives `T|error`, because only one wait on a strand succeeds and the others fail with an error
Know that if the awaited strand terminated abnormally (panicked), the wait itself completes with a panic carrying that error
Use `wait {a: f1, b: f2}` (or `wait {w1, w2}` with named workers) to wait for several futures and get a record whose fields hold each result
Use `wait f1 | f2` to get the first non-error result, or the error from the last strand to finish if all finish with errors
Know that only named workers and started strands can be waited for; a function's default worker cannot be
Request cancellation with `f.cancel()` from lang.future, which sets a flag that the strand checks whenever it yields, terminating it abnormally
Pause the current strand with `runtime:sleep(seconds)` (a decimal number of seconds), which yields; `runtime` is not a predeclared prefix, so `import ballerina/lang.runtime;` is required

nodes.title: Isolation
nodes.summary: The isolation model that guarantees data-race freedom through isolated functions, isolated objects and classes, isolated module variables, isolated expressions and compiler-inferred isolation.

must_cover.text: Explain the isolation guarantee: isolated objects and isolated variables are isolated roots whose freely reachable mutable state is accessed only under a lock statement, so there are no data races on it

Explain what calling an `isolated` function guarantees: it touches only mutable state reachable from its arguments (on the calling strand), state reachable from isolated variables or isolated objects, and new values it creates
Write `isolated function` bodies that call only isolated functions and methods, including an isolated `init` when using `new` or an object constructor (a missing init counts as isolated)

Know that an isolated function may read a non-isolated module-level identifier only if it is declared `final` or `configurable` (or by a listener or service declaration) and its static type is a subtype of `readonly` or `isolated object {}`, and may never assign a non-isolated module variable
Know that an anonymous function or named worker in an isolated function may only capture variables that are final and have a readonly or isolated-object type
Know that an isolated function may contain a `start` only when the started call is isolated
Declare `isolated` module variables, which must not be public, must bind a plain variable name and must have an isolated initializer, and access them only inside `lock`

Identify isolated expressions: any expression whose static type is readonly or an isolated object, list, mapping and table constructors, templates, casts, `check`, `trap` and conditional expressions whose subexpressions are isolated, range expressions, and calls to `clone` or `cloneReadOnly`

Define isolated objects with `isolated class C { ... }` or `isolated object { ... }`, where every field initializer must be isolated, fields that are not isolated (final with readonly or isolated-object type) must be `private`, and `self` must be used inside a `lock` except in `self.f` where `f` is an isolated field
Know that an object constructor is implicitly isolated (its isolated bit is set and its type intersected with `isolated object {}`) when it is implicitly readonly or all its fields are isolated
Know that an `isolated function` type admits only function values with the isolated bit set, and that a method value obtained by `obj.m` is isolated only if both the object and the method are
Know that an isolated function with an external body must itself access only mutable state reachable from its parameters and behave correctly when called concurrently from several strands

Explain isolated inference: the compiler may infer `isolated` for service declarations, object constructors (added in 2024R1), module variables, classes, functions and methods that would meet the rules, as an optimization that does not change types visible to other modules

Know why isolation matters: listeners can use the isolated bit of services and remote methods to call them concurrently, and named workers, forks and isolated starts in isolated functions may run on separate threads

nodes.title: Iterability
nodes.summary: Which basic types are iterable, their value and completion types, the built-in Iterator and Iterable object types, and the rules for mutating a structure while iterating it.

must_cover.text: Name the iterable basic types and their iteration sequences: string (length-1 substrings of type `string:Char`), xml (singleton items), lists and tables (members in order), mappings (members) and streams (items)
Explain the value type and completion type of an iterable type, with completion type `()` for all iterable types except `stream<T,C>`, whose completion type is `C`
Describe the Iterator object type `object { public function next() returns record {| T value; |}|C; }` and explain why `next` wraps each value in a record
Explain that `next()` returns an error if iteration hit an error, `()` once the end is reached, and otherwise advances and returns `{value: v}`, starting from the beginning position

Explain that `next()` panics if the structure was mutated after the iterator was created, except for removing a member already returned or changing the member for an existing key (in which case the current value is returned)
Obtain iterators explicitly with the langlib `iterator()` functions such as `arr.iterator()`, `m.iterator()`, `s.iterator()`, `x.iterator()`, `t.iterator()` and `stm.iterator()`
Make an object iterable by including the distinct type `object:Iterable` and defining an `iterator()` method that returns an Iterator, so it can be used in `foreach` and query `from` clauses
Distinguish built-in object types that are purely structural (such as Iterator) from distinct types named in a lang library module (such as `object:Iterable` and `object:RawTemplate`)

out_of_scope: foreach and while loops and range expressions (concept.loops)
nodes.notes: 5.1.6 lists the xml value type as `T` for `xml<T>`; the lang.object Iterable type's next returns `record {| any|error value; |}|error?`.

nodes.title: JSON and anydata
nodes.summary: The anydata type of plain data, the json type with lax static typing for field access and check, and the lang.value functions for converting between json, JSON text and user-defined types.

must_cover.text: Use `anydata` for plain data, equivalent to `() | boolean | int | float | decimal | string | xml | regexp:RegExp | anydata[] | map<anydata> | table<map<anydata>>`, which excludes errors, functions, objects and other behavioral values
Use `json`, the built-in union `() | boolean | int | float | decimal | string | json[] | map<json>`, to represent JSON data, writing JSON null as `()` or `null`
Explain that `json` is lax and `map<T>` is lax when T is lax, and that laxness only relaxes typing of field access, optional field access and `check`
Access json fields with `j.name` (or chains like `j.a.b`) without a cast, where the static type is `json|error` and the result is an error at runtime if the value is not a mapping or lacks the field
Use optional field access `j?.name` on json, which returns `()` when the value is nil or the field is missing and an error when the value is not a mapping

Write `int age = check j.age;`, where `check` on a lax expression whose expected type is a simple type is treated as `check value:ensureType(j.age, int)`, failing with an error if the value has the wrong type

Convert anydata to json with `v.toJson()`, a deep copy that turns xml into a string and tables into lists of mappings, gives arrays and maps inherent types `json[]` and `map<json>`, copies even immutable values, and panics on cyclic values
Serialize with `v.toJsonString()`, which first converts the value as `toJson` does and returns JSON text

Parse JSON text with `value:fromJsonString(s)` (or `s.fromJsonString()`), which returns an error on invalid input and maps numbers to int when they have integer syntax and fit in int, to float `-0.0` for negative zero, and to decimal otherwise
Use `fromJsonFloatString` and `fromJsonDecimalString` to parse JSON numbers uniformly as float (`value:JsonFloat`) or decimal (`value:JsonDecimal`)

Convert json to a user type with `j.fromJsonWithType(T)` or `T x = check j.fromJsonWithType();`, which works like cloneWithType plus the inverse of toJson conversions, and use `fromJsonStringWithType` to parse and convert in one step
Use `value:mergeJson(j1, j2)` which returns j2 if j1 is nil, j1 if j2 is nil, recursively merges two mappings key by key (mutating j1), and otherwise returns an error leaving j1 unchanged
Explain that an inclusive record type `record { ... }` allows extra fields only of type anydata, i.e. it is `record {| ...; anydata...; |}`

out_of_scope: Record and map types in general (concept.records, concept.maps)
nodes.notes: 5.6.10 says plain data includes tagged data values; since `re` is the only data tag in 2024R1 all tagged data values belong to regexp:RegExp.

nodes.title: Lang library
nodes.summary: The `ballerina/lang.*` modules defined by the specification, one per basic type plus `lang.value`, `lang.transaction` and `lang.runtime`, that provide the fundamental operations on language values.

must_cover.text: Use `lang.array` (basic type list) functions `length`, `iterator`, `enumerate`, `map`, `forEach`, `filter`, `reduce`, `some`, `every`, `slice`, `remove`, `removeAll`, `setLength`, `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf`, `reverse`, `sort` (with `SortDirection` and `OrderedType`), `pop`, `push`, `shift`, `unshift`, `toBase64`/`fromBase64`, `toBase16`/`fromBase16` and `toStream`

Use `lang.boolean` functions `boolean:fromString` (accepts `true`/`false` in any letter case and `1`/`0`, otherwise returns an error), `boolean:some` (false when given no arguments) and `boolean:every` (true when given no arguments)
Use `lang.decimal` (basic type decimal) functions `sum`, `max`, `min`, `avg`, `abs`, `round`, `quantize`, `floor`, `ceiling` and `fromString` on decimal values

Use `lang.error` (basic type error) functions `message`, `cause`, `detail` (returns an immutable detail record), `stackTrace`, `toString` and `toBalString`, and the types it defines: `Cloneable`, `Detail`, `StackFrame`, the distinct error types `NoMessage` and `Retriable`, and the class `DefaultRetryManager`

Use `lang.float` (basic type float) constants `PI`, `E`, `NaN` and `Infinity` and its functions for classification (`isFinite`, `isInfinite`, `isNaN`), aggregation (`sum`, `max`, `min`, `avg`), rounding (`abs`, `round`, `floor`, `ceiling`), maths (`sqrt`, `cbrt`, `pow`, `log`, `log10`, `exp`, trigonometric and hyperbolic functions), parsing and formatting (`fromString`, `toHexString`, `fromHexString`, `toFixedString`, `toExpString`) and bit conversion (`toBitsInt`, `fromBitsInt`)
Use `function:call(func, ...args)` from `lang.function` (basic type function) to call a function value dynamically, knowing that it panics if the arguments are not of the types `func` requires
Use `future:cancel(f)` from `lang.future` (basic type future) to set the cancellation flag of the strand behind a future, which then terminates abnormally the next time it yields

Use `lang.int` (basic type int) built-in subtypes `Signed8`, `Signed16`, `Signed32`, `Unsigned8`, `Unsigned16`, `Unsigned32`, its range constants (`MAX_VALUE`, `MIN_VALUE`, `SIGNED32_MAX_VALUE` and so on), and its functions `abs`, `sum`, `max`, `min`, `avg`, `fromString`, `toHexString`, `fromHexString` and `range`

Use `lang.map` (basic type mapping) functions `length`, `iterator`, `get` (panics if the key is missing), `entries`, `map`, `forEach`, `filter`, `reduce`, `remove` (panics if the key is missing), `removeIfHasKey`, `removeAll`, `hasKey`, `keys` and `toArray`

Use the distinct object types defined by `lang.object` (basic type object): `object:Iterable`, whose `iterator()` method makes an object iterable, and `object:RawTemplate`, with fields `strings` (`readonly & string[]`) and `insertions` (`(any|error)[]`), the type of raw template values

Use the preview `lang.regexp` module for the `re` tagged data type: the `RegExp` type, `Span` and `Groups`, matching functions `find`, `findGroups`, `findAll`, `findAllGroups`, `matchAt`, `matchGroupsAt`, `isFullMatch` and `fullMatchGroups`, replacement with `replace`/`replaceAll` taking a `Replacement` (a string or `ReplacerFunction`), `split` and `fromString`

Use `lang.stream` (basic type stream) functions `iterator`, `next`, `close`, `map`, `forEach`, `filter` and `reduce` on `stream<T,C>` values, where `forEach` returns the stream's completion value and `reduce` returns the combined result or the stream's error

Use `lang.string` (basic type string) and its built-in subtype `string:Char` with functions for length and iteration, concatenation and joining, substrings and code points, searching, ASCII case handling, trimming and padding, UTF-8 and code-point conversion, and regular-expression matching (`matches`, `includesMatch`)

Use `lang.table` (basic type table) functions `length`, `iterator`, `get` (panics if the key is missing), `put` (replaces a member with the same key, keeping its position), `add` (panics on a duplicate key), `map` (result is `key<never>`), `forEach`, `filter` (keeps the same keys), `reduce`, `remove`, `removeIfHasKey`, `removeAll`, `hasKey`, `keys`, `toArray` and `nextKey` (maximum used int key + 1, or 0)

Use `typedesc:typeIds(t, primaryOnly)` from `lang.typedesc` (basic type typedesc) to get the type-ids induced by a typedesc as `readonly & TypeId[]` (each with a `ModuleId` and a `localId` of type `string|int`), or nil if `t` is not definite

Use `lang.xml` (basic type xml) built-in subtypes `Element`, `ProcessingInstruction`, `Comment` and `Text`, the namespace constants (`XML_NAMESPACE_URI`, `XMLNS_NAMESPACE_URI`, `space`, `lang`, `base`), and its functions for access, construction, selection, transformation and parsing (`fromString`)

Use `lang.transaction`, which does not correspond to a basic type, inside transactional code: `info()`, `getInfo(xid)`, `setRollbackOnly`, `getRollbackOnly`, `setData`/`getData`, and `onCommit`/`onRollback` with `CommitHandler`/`RollbackHandler`, plus the types `Info`, `Timestamp` and `transaction:Error` (the commit action's error type), knowing that the `transactional` functions can be called only in a transactional scope

Use `lang.runtime`, which does not correspond to a basic type: `runtime:sleep(seconds)` (decimal seconds; makes the current strand yield), `registerListener`/`deregisterListener` with `DynamicListener`, `getStackTrace` returning `StackFrame[]`, and `onGracefulStop` with a `StopHandler`

Use `lang.value`, whose functions work on values of more than one basic type: `clone`, `cloneReadOnly`, `cloneWithType`, `ensureType`, `toString`, `toBalString`, `fromBalString`, `toJson`, `toJsonString`, `fromJsonString`, `fromJsonFloatString`, `fromJsonDecimalString`, `fromJsonWithType`, `fromJsonStringWithType`, `mergeJson`, `count`, `first` and `last`, and the types `Cloneable`, `JsonFloat` and `JsonDecimal`

out_of_scope: The Ballerina standard library (ballerina/http, ballerina/io, ...), which the spec explicitly does not specify
Generic typing annotations, built-in subtypes and method-call dispatch rules (concept.langlib_conventions)
Detailed function semantics for array, string, int/float/decimal, xml and regexp (concept.langlib_array, concept.langlib_string, concept.langlib_numeric, concept.langlib_xml, concept.langlib_regexp)

Detailed map, table, stream, error, value, transaction and runtime semantics, which are covered by the topic nodes that use them (maps, tables, streams, errors, value_cloning, json_anydata, string_conversion, transactions, services_listeners)
nodes.notes: lang.regexp is marked (preview) in 2024R1. Modules in the `ballerina` organization whose names start with `lang.` are reserved for the lang library. In lang.transaction, the types `Error` and `Info` are written without `public` in the spec text even though the commit action's type is `transaction:Error?`; treat them as part of the module's API. The lang.table iterator doc comment mentions an `entries` function that lang.table does not define.

nodes.title: lang.array
nodes.summary: Detailed semantics of the `lang.array` module's functions on list values, including which ones mutate in place, which return new arrays, and which panic.

must_cover.text: Use `arr.length()` to get the number of members and `arr.iterator()` to get an iterator object whose `next()` returns `record {| T value; |}` or nil at the end
Mutate an array at its end with `push(...vals)` (appends values) and `pop()` (removes and returns the last member; the array must not be empty)
Mutate an array at its start with `shift()` (removes and returns the first member; the array must not be empty) and `unshift(...vals)` (adds values at the start, keeping them in the order given)
Remove members with `remove(index)` (returns the removed member and panics if there is no member at `index`) and `removeAll()` (panics if any member cannot be removed)
Change an array's length in place with `setLength(n)`, knowing that `setLength(arr, 0)` is equivalent to `removeAll(arr)`

Use `slice(startIndex, endIndex = arr.length())` to get a new array with the members whose index is >= startIndex and < endIndex, and `reverse()` to get a new array in reverse order without modifying the original
Search with `indexOf(val, startIndex = 0)` and `lastIndexOf(val, startIndex = arr.length() - 1)`, which compare using `==`, return `int?` (nil when not found) and require an array of anydata members

Apply functions to members in order with `map` (new array of results), `filter` (new array of members for which the predicate returns true) and `forEach` (for side effects), passing function values or arrow functions such as `arr.map(x => x * 2)`

Combine members with `reduce(func, initial)`, where `func` takes the accumulated value and a member and returns the new accumulated value, e.g. `reduce([1, 2, 3], function (int total, int n) returns int { return total + n; }, 0)`
Test members with `some(func)`, which stops at the first true result and returns false for an empty array, and `every(func)`, which stops at the first false result and returns true for an empty array
Use `enumerate()` to get a new array of `[int, T]` index-member pairs, e.g. for `foreach [int, string] [i, s] in names.enumerate()`

Sort with `sort(direction = array:ASCENDING, key = ())`, which returns a new sorted array, takes `array:DESCENDING` for descending order, and needs a `key` function returning an `OrderedType` when the member type is not ordered (e.g. sorting records by a field)
Explain that `sort` orders members the same way as the `order by` clause of query expressions, so nil and NaN go at the end in both directions and equal keys keep their original relative order
Explain `array:OrderedType` (`()|boolean|int|float|decimal|string|OrderedType[]`) as a necessary but not sufficient condition for a type to be ordered

Convert `byte[]` to and from text with `toBase64`/`fromBase64` and `toBase16`/`fromBase16`, where the `to` functions produce strings without whitespace (Base16 uses lower-case `a..f`) and the `from` functions return `byte[]|error`
Use `toStream()` to get a `stream<T,()>` over an array's members, which uses an iterator over the array and so handles mutation of the array the same way an iterator does

out_of_scope: Array and tuple types, list constructors and indexing (concept.arrays_tuples)
nodes.notes: Stable ordering of equal keys comes from 6.35.6, where entries with equal keys keep their input order; `sort` is defined to work like the query sort clause. The spec does not say which inherent types make `removeAll` panic (e.g. fixed-length arrays); the item keeps only the stated rule. The `toStream` doc comment has a garbled sentence ('Theutation of the `arr`') and uses an undeclared type parameter `T`.

nodes.title: Langlib conventions
nodes.summary: How lang library modules express generic typing with annotations, define built-in subtypes, and are reached through predeclared module prefixes and method-call syntax.

must_cover.text: Explain the `@typeParam` annotation: a lang library type definition marked with it acts as a type parameter, so every use of it within one function declaration (e.g. `Type` in `push(Type[] arr, Type... vals)`) refers to the same type, and its definition is an upper bound

Explain the `@isolatedParam` annotation on a function-typed parameter of an isolated langlib function: when the call must be isolated, the argument supplied (e.g. the callback to `map` or `filter`) must also be isolated
Explain that Ballerina 2024R1 has no user-defined generic types, which is why the lang library expresses generics through annotations
