List the built-in subtypes and their ranges: `int:Signed8` (-128..127), `int:Signed16` (-32,768..32,767), `int:Signed32` (-2,147,483,648..2,147,483,647), `int:Unsigned8` (0..255), `int:Unsigned16` (0..65,535), `int:Unsigned32` (0..4,294,967,295), `string:Char` (length 1), and `xml:Element`, `xml:ProcessingInstruction`, `xml:Comment` and `xml:Text` (empty or a text singleton)
Reference a built-in subtype `T` of basic type `B` with a qualified type reference `M:T` where `M` refers to `ballerina/lang.B`, and know that `int:Unsigned8` is equivalent to the predefined `byte`

Explain that `@builtinSubtype` marks a lang library type definition whose meaning comes from the specification rather than from its type descriptor (e.g. `@builtinSubtype type Signed32 int;`), and that using it outside the lang library is an error

Use the predeclared module prefixes `boolean`, `decimal`, `error`, `float`, `function`, `future`, `int`, `map`, `object`, `stream`, `string`, `table`, `transaction`, `typedesc` and `xml`, which refer to the corresponding `lang.*` module without an import and without a quoted identifier (e.g. `int:fromString(s)`)

Override a predeclared prefix with an `import` declaration that binds the same prefix to another module, and import modules without a predeclared prefix, such as `ballerina/lang.array`, `ballerina/lang.value`, `ballerina/lang.regexp` and `ballerina/lang.runtime`, explicitly

Explain how `v.f(args)` on a non-object value becomes the lang library call `m:f(v, args)`, where `m` is `lang.B` if the static type of `v` is a subtype of basic type B and `lang.B` defines `f`, and `lang.value` otherwise (e.g. `[1,2].length()` calls `array:length`, `x.toString()` calls `value:toString`)

Explain that a method call converted to a lang library call must satisfy every constraint of the equivalent function call (a compile error otherwise), and is isolated under the same conditions as that function call

Explain that a call `f(x)` where `f` is unqualified and the only argument is an aggregated variable of type `T` (e.g. `sum(price)` after `group by` or in `collect`) resolves `f` in `lang.B` when `T` is a subtype of `B[]` and `lang.B` defines `f`, and in `lang.value` otherwise (e.g. `count`, `first`, `last`)

Explain that when such a langlib function needs at least one argument but the aggregated list may be empty (e.g. `max(x)` in a `collect` clause), the call returns nil for an empty list and its return type is unioned with nil

Explain that modules in the `ballerina` organization whose names start with `lang.` are reserved for the lang library defined by the specification, and that every module except `lang.value`, `lang.transaction` and `lang.runtime` corresponds to a basic type

out_of_scope: General import syntax and module prefixes (concept.modules_imports)
nodes.notes: Spec 11.1 says generic types are planned for a future version. The lang.int doc comments for Signed16 and Signed8 say 'non-negative integers' but then give signed ranges (-2^15..2^15-1, -2^7..2^7-1); the 11.2 table and the ranges are taken as authoritative. Saying that `lang.array`, `lang.value`, `lang.regexp` and `lang.runtime` are not predeclared is derived from the predeclared-prefix list in 8.1, which omits them; the spec does not say this explicitly.

nodes.title: lang.int/float/decimal
nodes.summary: Constants and functions of the numeric lang library modules for aggregation, rounding, maths, parsing, formatting and bit-level conversion of int, float and decimal values.

must_cover.text: Use the `lang.int` constants `int:MAX_VALUE` (9223372036854775807), `int:MIN_VALUE` (defined as `-9223372036854775807 - 1` because the literal 9223372036854775808 would overflow) and the subtype bounds `SIGNED32_MAX_VALUE`, `SIGNED32_MIN_VALUE`, `SIGNED16_*`, `SIGNED8_*` and `UNSIGNED32/16/8_MAX_VALUE`
Use `int:abs`, `int:sum(...ns)` (0 for no arguments), `int:max(n, ...ns)` and `int:min(n, ...ns)`, which need at least one argument
Use `int:avg(n, ...ns)`, which computes the average with the decimal type, returns `decimal` (not int) and panics if the sum overflows decimal

Parse and format ints with `int:fromString(s)` (decimal digits with an optional leading `+` or `-`; returns an error otherwise), `toHexString()` (lower-case, no `0x` prefix, `-` prefix for negatives) and `int:fromHexString(s)` (upper- or lower-case digits, optional sign, no `0x`/`0X` prefix allowed)
Use `int:range(start, end, step)` to get an `object:Iterable` over `start + step*i` that is increasing and < end when step > 0, decreasing and > end when step < 0, and panics when step is 0
Use the `lang.float` constants `float:PI`, `float:E`, `float:NaN` (`0.0/0.0`) and `float:Infinity` (`1.0/0.0`)
Classify floats with `isNaN`, `isFinite` and `isInfinite`, exactly one of which is true for any float value

Use `float:sum`, `float:max`, `float:min` and `float:avg`, which take zero or more arguments: `sum` of no arguments is +0.0, `max` is -∞, `min` is +∞ and `avg` is NaN, and `sum`, `max` and `min` return NaN if any argument is NaN
Use `decimal:sum(...xs)` (0 for no arguments) and `decimal:max`, `decimal:min` and `decimal:avg`, which require at least one argument

Round with `round(fractionDigits = 0)` on float and decimal values, which rounds to the nearest multiple of 10^-fractionDigits with ties to even (e.g. `2.5.round()` is 2.0), and use `floor`, `ceiling` and `abs`; float `round` returns NaN, ±0 and ±∞ unchanged
Explain that converting with `<int>x` is the same as `<int>x.round(0)` for both float and decimal, so the conversion rounds half to even rather than truncating

Use `decimal:quantize(x, y)` (the IEEE quantize operation) to get a value equal to `x` (apart from rounding) with the exponent of `y`, e.g. to fix a decimal to two fraction digits, and contrast `decimal:round` with fractionDigits 0 with IEEE roundToIntegralTiesToEven, which keeps a positive exponent

Use the float maths functions that correspond to IEEE operations: `sqrt`, `cbrt`, `pow(x, y)`, `log`, `log10`, `exp`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2(y, x)`, `sinh`, `cosh` and `tanh` (results in radians where relevant)

Parse numbers with `float:fromString` (DecimalFloatingPointNumber syntax with an optional sign, also `NaN` and `Infinity` with an optional sign, no `f`/`d` suffix) and `decimal:fromString` (optional sign, no suffix, no NaN or Infinity), both returning `T|error`
Use `float:toHexString` (HexFloatingPointLiteral form with `0x` for finite values, a `-` sign when negative, and `Infinity`, `-Infinity` and `NaN` for the special values) and `float:fromHexString`
Use `toBitsInt` and `float:fromBitsInt` to convert between a float and its IEEE 64-bit binary representation as an int, knowing that every NaN bit pattern maps to the single float NaN value

Format floats with `toFixedString(fractionDigits)` (no exponent) and `toExpString(fractionDigits)` (one digit before the point and a lower-case `e` exponent with a sign and at least two digits), where `()` means the minimum digits needed, 0 means no decimal point, rounding is ties-to-even, NaN and infinities format as `value:toString` does, and a negative fractionDigits panics

out_of_scope: Numeric types, literals, ranges and NumericConvert (concept.numeric_types)
nodes.notes: Spec doc-comment issues: lang.int Signed16/Signed8 comments say 'non-negative' but give signed ranges; `int:max` and `int:avg` return docs mention `x`/`xs` and 'minimum value' (copy-paste errors); float `ceiling`'s return doc says 'decimal value'. The `2.5.round()` example is derived from the stated ties-to-even rule, not quoted from the spec. The spec does not say what `round` does with a negative fractionDigits.

nodes.title: lang.regexp
nodes.summary: The preview `lang.regexp` module's types and functions for finding, matching, replacing and splitting with `re` regular expressions.

must_cover.text: Use `regexp:RegExp`, the built-in subtype naming the tagged data basic type for tag `re`, as the type of `re`...`` values and of function parameters that take regular expressions
Use a `regexp:Span`, a readonly object with `startIndex`, `endIndex` (the index after the end, so the length is `endIndex - startIndex`) and a `substring()` method that returns the matched text

Use `regexp:Groups` (`readonly & [Span, Span?...]`), where member 0 is the match of the whole regular expression and member i is the i-th capturing group (groups ordered by the position of their opening parenthesis), which is nil if the match did not use that group
Find the first match at or after `startIndex` (default 0) with `re.find(str, startIndex)` returning `Span?`, or with `findGroups` returning `Groups?`
Find all matches with `findAll` (returns `Span[]`) and `findAllGroups` (returns `Groups[]`), knowing that each search continues where the previous match ended, so matches never overlap
Test for a match that starts exactly at an index with `matchAt(str, startIndex = 0)` (returns `Span?` whose `startIndex` equals the given index) or `matchGroupsAt` (returns `Groups?`)

Test whether a regular expression matches the whole string (from index 0 to its length) with `isFullMatch(str)`, or get the groups of such a match with `fullMatchGroups(str)`, which returns nil if there is no full match

Replace the first match with `replace(str, replacement, startIndex = 0)` and every non-overlapping match with `replaceAll(str, replacement, startIndex = 0)`, where `replacement` is a `Replacement` (a fixed string or a `ReplacerFunction`)
Write a `ReplacerFunction` (`isolated function(Groups groups) returns string`) that builds each replacement from the match's groups, e.g. to reformat captured dates
Split a string with `re.split(str)`, which returns the substrings before the first match, between matches and after the last match of the separator pattern, or `[str]` if nothing matches
Build a regular expression at runtime with `regexp:fromString(str)`, which accepts the same syntax as the `re` template and returns an error if `str` is not a valid regular expression

Explain that `matchGroupsAt` corresponds to the ECMAScript abstract matching function and that `matchAt`, `find`, `findGroups`, `findAll`, `findAllGroups`, the full-match functions and `isFullMatch` can be defined in terms of it

out_of_scope: Regular expression syntax, flags, the `re` template and interpolation (concept.regexp)
nodes.notes: lang.regexp is preview in 2024R1. Spec typos: the `Groups` doc comment says 'The group with index i, where i > 1, is the i-th capturing group' (should read i >= 1); section 10.1 refers to a `fullMatchGroup` function while the module defines `fullMatchGroups`; the `findAllGroups` return doc says 'a `Group`' for each match. The spec does not say what happens for an out-of-range `startIndex`.

nodes.title: lang.string
nodes.summary: Detailed semantics of the `lang.string` module's functions for measuring, slicing, searching, comparing, case-converting, padding, encoding and regex-matching strings.

must_cover.text: Use `str.length()`, which counts characters (code points), and iterate over a string with `foreach` or `str.iterator()`, which yields length-1 substrings of type `string:Char` in order
Use the built-in subtype `string:Char` for single-character strings, e.g. as the type of `padChar` and of `toCodePointInt`'s parameter
Combine strings with `string:concat(...strs)` (empty string for no arguments) and `string:'join(separator, ...strs)` (separator placed between the strings)
Extract text with `substring(startIndex, endIndex = str.length())`, which returns the characters with index >= startIndex and < endIndex

Search with `indexOf(substr, startIndex = 0)` (first occurrence at or after startIndex) and `lastIndexOf(substr, startIndex = str.length() - substr.length())` (last occurrence at or before startIndex), which return `int?` with nil when not found, and with `includes(substr, startIndex = 0)`
Test prefixes and suffixes with `startsWith(substr)` and `endsWith(substr)`
Change case with `toLowerAscii` and `toUpperAscii`, which convert only A-Z/a-z and leave other characters unchanged, and compare case-insensitively with `equalsIgnoreCaseAscii`
Use `trim()` to remove ASCII white space (0x9 to 0xD and 0x20) from both ends of a string

Compare strings with `codePointCompare(str1, str2)`, which returns a negative, zero or positive int by lexicographic Unicode code point order, and know that this order often differs from culturally expected sort order

Convert between strings and code points with `getCodePoint(index)`, `toCodePointInts()`, `toCodePointInt(ch)`, `fromCodePointInts(ints)` and `fromCodePointInt(cp)`, where the `from` functions return an error for an invalid code point (outside 0 to 0x10FFFF or in the surrogate range 0xD800 to 0xDFFF)
Encode a string to UTF-8 with `toBytes()` returning `byte[]` and decode with `string:fromBytes(bytes)`, which returns `string|error`
Pad strings to a length with `padStart(len, padChar = " ")` and `padEnd(len, padChar = " ")`, which return `str` unchanged when its length is already >= `len`
Use `padZero(len, zeroChar = "0")` to add zeros at the start of a string but after a leading `+` or `-` sign, e.g. for formatting numbers to a fixed width

Match strings against `re` regular expressions with `str.matches(re)`, which requires a full match (equivalent to `regexp:isFullMatch(re, str)`), and `str.includesMatch(re, startIndex = 0)`, which accepts a match anywhere (equivalent to `regexp:find(re, str, startIndex) != ()`)

out_of_scope: String literals, escapes, string templates and immutability (concept.strings)
Converting other values to strings and parsing numbers (concept.string_conversion, concept.langlib_numeric)
Regular expression syntax and the full lang.regexp API (concept.regexp, concept.langlib_regexp)
nodes.notes: The doc comment for `matches` says it is equivalent to `regex:isFullMatch`; the module prefix is spelled `regex` there (a typo for `regexp`). The spec does not say whether `substring` or `getCodePoint` panic on out-of-range indexes, so no such claim is made.

nodes.title: lang.xml
nodes.summary: The `lang.xml` module's constants, built-in subtypes and functions for accessing, constructing, selecting, transforming and parsing xml values.

must_cover.text: Use the constants `xml:XML_NAMESPACE_URI`, `xml:XMLNS_NAMESPACE_URI` and the expanded attribute names `xml:space`, `xml:lang` and `xml:base` (e.g. `"{http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace}lang"`)
Use `x.length()` for the number of items in an xml sequence and iterate with `foreach` or `x.iterator()`, where each item is an xml singleton

Use `x.get(i)` to get the item at index `i`, and distinguish it from `x[i]`: `get` panics when there is no item with that index, whereas `x[i]` returns empty xml for an index >= the length (and panics only for a negative index)
Build sequences with `xml:concat(...xs)`, which concatenates xml and string values (strings become text) and returns an empty xml sequence when given no arguments
Read and change an element's expanded name with `getName()` and `setName(xName)`
Use `getAttributes()` to get an element's attributes as `map<string>` keyed by expanded attribute names, including namespace attributes
Read and replace an element's children with `getChildren()` and `setChildren(xml|string)`, knowing that `setChildren` panics if it would make the element structure cyclic
Use `getDescendants()` to get the children together with, recursively, the descendants of each child element, in document order (each element immediately precedes its descendants)

Use `xml:data(x)` to get the character data of an xml value: text characters and, recursively, element content, with comments, processing instructions and empty sequences contributing the empty string
Use `getTarget()` on a processing instruction and `getContent()` on a processing instruction or comment

Construct items with `xml:createElement(name, attributes = {}, children = xml``)` (copies the attributes into a new map), `xml:createProcessingInstruction(target, content)`, `xml:createComment(content)` and `xml:createText(data)`, which returns empty xml for an empty string
Use `slice(startIndex, endIndex = x.length())` to get the subsequence of items with index >= startIndex and < endIndex
Use `strip()` to remove comments, processing instructions and text items consisting entirely of XML white space (the S production of XML 1.0) from an xml sequence

Select items with `elements(nm = ())` (element items, optionally only those with expanded name `nm`), `children()` (equivalent to `elements(x).map(getChildren)`), `elementChildren(nm = ())` (equivalent to `children(x).elements(nm)`) and `text()` (the concatenated text items)
Transform xml sequences item by item with `map` (returns `xml<XmlType>`), `forEach` and `filter`, where each item is passed as a singleton
Parse XML text with `xml:fromString(s)`, which parses using the XML 1.0 `content` production and returns `xml|error`

out_of_scope: xml types, the xml template and xml concatenation with + (concept.xml)

edges.note: XML step expressions are defined in terms of xml:map, xml:elements, xml:getChildren and xml:getDescendants

nodes.notes: The empty-xml result of `x[i]` comes from 6.14 (member access); the `get` doc comment only says that `get` panics where `x[i]` does not. The `xml:Text` doc comment says 'singleton test sequence' (a typo for text).

nodes.title: Lexical structure
nodes.summary: How Ballerina source is decoded and tokenized, including identifier forms, quoted and escaped identifiers, restricted identifiers, comments and white space.

must_cover.text: Explain that a module source part is decoded as UTF-8 (RFC 3629), a leading byte order mark (0xFEFF) is removed, and CR LF and lone CR are normalized to LF before parsing
List the code points that must not occur in source, namely surrogates, the 66 Unicode noncharacters, C0 controls other than tab, LF, form feed and CR, and C1 controls (0x80 to 0x9F)
Write unquoted identifiers that start with an ASCII letter, `_` or a non-ASCII identifier character and continue with those characters or digits

Explain that non-ASCII characters are allowed in identifiers except private-use characters, Pattern_White_Space and Pattern_Syntax characters, following Unicode TR31 immutable identifiers so the allowed set does not change between Unicode versions
Use a quoted identifier `'K` (a single quote before the name) to use a reserved keyword K as an identifier, for example a field or variable named `'type`

Use identifier escapes, a backslash before a non-letter, non-whitespace character (e.g. `first\-name`) or a numeric escape `\u{XXXX}`, so any non-empty string can be an identifier, and know the numeric escape must be a valid non-surrogate code point up to 0x10FFFF
Explain that organization and module names must be restricted identifiers made of ASCII letters and digits starting with a letter, with single underscores only between letter/digit runs
Write comments with `//`, which run to the end of the line; this is the only comment form defined by the grammar
Explain that white space (tab, LF, CR, space) and comments may appear between tokens of lower-case grammar productions, but not inside tokens of upper-case (lexical) productions
Explain the NoSpaceColon rule, that no white space is allowed before or after the colon in a qualified identifier such as `io:println` or an XML qualified name `ns:name`

Recognize that some keywords are marked NR (not reserved) in the grammar, such as the query clause keywords `where`, `join`, `outer`, `limit`, `order`, `by`, `group`, `collect`, `select` and `conflict`, and so can still be used as identifiers

sources.note: 6.35 query clause productions use NR keywords

nodes.notes: Spec 4 says C0 controls are '0x0 to 0x1F and 0x1F' (duplicated bound) and allows 0xC (form feed) as white space in the disallowed-list text although WhiteSpaceChar only lists 0x9, 0xA, 0xD, 0x20. The spec has no consolidated list of reserved keywords; NR keywords are inferred from the productions marked NR (where, join, outer, limit, order, by, group, collect, select, conflict). B.2 states clause keywords except `from` and `let` are no longer reserved.

nodes.title: Lock
nodes.summary: The lock statement, which runs a block as if not interleaved with other locks, and the restrictions that apply when it guards isolated variables or isolated object state.

must_cover.text: Use `lock { ... }` so that the block's effect on program state is as if it were not interleaved with any lock statement executing on another strand
Explain that a lock behaves like acquiring one program-wide recursive mutex around the block, while implementations may infer finer-grained locking with the same effect
Know that `start` and named worker declarations are compile-time errors lexically inside a lock, and that starting a strand while a lock is held panics
Know that a lock statement may not contain a sync send action (`->>`) or a receive action (`<-`), a restriction added in 2024R1
Access an `isolated` module-level variable only inside a lock statement
In the methods of an isolated object, access `self.x` inside a lock unless field `x` is isolated (final with a readonly or isolated-object type)
Know that a lock statement may use at most one restricted variable (an isolated module variable or `self` of an isolated object)
Know that inside a lock using a restricted variable only functions and methods with isolated types may be called

Apply the transfer-out rules: a `return` inside the lock must return an isolated expression, and an assignment to a variable defined outside must have a plain variable name on the left and an isolated expression on the right (assigning the restricted variable itself is exempt)

Apply the transfer-in rule: a reference to a variable or parameter defined outside the lock must occur within an isolated expression (for example `x.clone()` or a readonly value), and in a non-isolated object `self` is treated like a parameter

out_of_scope: Isolated functions, objects and variables in general (concept.isolation)

nodes.title: Logical expressions
nodes.summary: The boolean operators `!`, `&&` and `||` with short-circuit evaluation, the ternary conditional `? :` and the nil-conditional (Elvis) operator `?:`.

must_cover.text: Use `!` on a boolean operand to negate it, with result type boolean (singleton when the operand is singleton)
Combine boolean expressions with `&&` and `||`, whose operands must be subtypes of boolean
Explain short-circuit evaluation, that the right operand of `&&` is not evaluated when the left is false and the right operand of `||` is not evaluated when the left is true
Explain that `&&` with a left operand of singleton type `false` has static type `false`, and `||` with a left operand of singleton type `true` has static type `true`, regardless of the right operand
Use the ternary conditional `cond ? a : b`, where cond must be boolean and only the selected branch is evaluated
Explain that the ternary's static type is the union of both branch types, or just one branch's type when the condition has singleton type `true` or `false`
Use the nil-conditional operator `x ?: d` to supply a default when x evaluates to nil, with the right operand evaluated only when needed
Explain that `L ?: R` has static type R when L's type is nil, L's type when it cannot be nil, and otherwise the union of L's type without nil and R's type
Explain that `?:` and `? :` are right-associative and bind more loosely than `||`, so `a ?: b ?: c` is `a ?: (b ?: c)`

nodes.title: Loops
nodes.summary: Iteration with foreach over any iterable value, while loops, break and continue, and integer range expressions.

must_cover.text: Iterate with `foreach T x in expr { ... }` or `foreach var x in expr { ... }` over any iterable value (list, mapping, table, string, xml, stream or Iterable object), with `var` inferring the iteration value type
Use a binding pattern in foreach, such as `foreach var [i, v] in arr.enumerate()` or `foreach var [k, v] in m.entries()`, knowing the compiler must be able to guarantee the pattern matches
Explain how foreach executes: it creates an iterator with `iterator()`, calls `next()` until it returns nil, and binds the `value` field of each result to the binding pattern
Know that variables bound by a foreach are implicitly final and scoped to the loop body
Know that foreach requires an iterable whose iteration completion type is nil, so iterating a `stream<T, error?>` with foreach is a compile-time error
Write `while cond { ... }` loops, where the boolean condition is re-evaluated before each iteration
Use `break;` to make the nearest enclosing while or foreach complete normally, and know it is allowed only lexically inside one
Use `continue;` to end the current iteration of the nearest enclosing while or foreach and go on with the next one, allowed only lexically inside a loop
Use range expressions `a ... b` (inclusive) and `a ..< b` (exclusive) with int operands, as in `foreach int i in 0 ..< n`, which produce an `Iterable<int,()>` object iterating in increasing order
Know that a range expression is an ordinary iterable object usable outside foreach, is always isolated, yields nothing when the start is past the end, and is a compile error with non-int operands
Use `int:range(start, end, step)` for stepped or descending iteration, which excludes `end` and panics when `step` is 0

Explain that mutating a list or mapping while iterating it makes the iterator's `next()` panic, except for removing a member already returned or changing the value at an existing key (in which case the new value is returned)

out_of_scope: Query expressions as an alternative to loops (concept.query_expressions)
on fail clauses attached to loops (concept.error_handling)

nodes.title: Maps
nodes.summary: Mapping values keyed by strings, described by map<T> types and built with mapping constructor expressions that support shorthand, computed-name, spread and readonly fields.

must_cover.text: Declare `map<T>` types, where every field value must belong to `T` and every key is a string, e.g. `map<int> ages = {alice: 30};`
Construct mappings with `{name: value}` fields using either a field name or a string literal key (`{"first name": "Ann"}`), and use the shorthand `{x}` as equivalent to `{x: x}`
Use spread fields `{...m, extra: 1}` to copy all fields of another mapping, and explain the compile error when a spread could duplicate a specific field or a field of another spread

Use computed-name fields `[keyExpr]: value`, whose key expression has contextually expected type `string`, and explain that they are applied in order after the rest of the mapping is built and panic if incompatible with the inherent type

Explain how a mapping constructor takes its inherent type from the contextually expected type, and how in a union the members inconsistent with the specific-field names are discarded so that exactly one mapping type must remain

Explain that with no contextually expected type the constructor infers an exclusive record type with one field per specific field (broad type, or precise type for readonly fields), adds spread types, and adds a rest descriptor for computed-name fields

Mark individual fields with `readonly` in a constructor (`{readonly id: 1}`), and know the whole mapping is constructed immutable when the applicable expected type is a subtype of `readonly`, with read-only bits set only after construction completes
Explain that when the expected type allows field `x` but not nil for it, a constructor value for `x` may be nil and then no `x` field is added
Explain that each field has its own read-only bit, a read-only field can be neither assigned nor removed, and a read-only mapping makes all its fields read-only
Explain that the inherent type of a mapping is enforced at runtime, so writing a field value that does not belong to the declared field type (e.g. through a `map<any>` view of a `map<int>`) panics

Iterate over a map with `foreach`, and explain that for map-typed values the order is the order fields were added (constructor order, computed-name fields last) while for record-typed values it is implementation-dependent
Use `m.get(k)` (panics if the key is missing), `m.hasKey(k)`, `m.remove(k)` (panics if missing), `m.removeIfHasKey(k)` and `m.removeAll()` from `lang.map`
Use `lang.map` functions `length`, `keys`, `toArray`, `entries` (returns `map<[string, T]>`), `map`, `filter`, `reduce` and `forEach` on mappings

out_of_scope: Record type descriptors and default values (concept.records)
Member access m[k], field access and optional field access (concept.field_member_access)
nodes.notes: Mapping constructor grammar allows `[readonly] variable-name` shorthand as well as `[readonly] field-name: value`.

nodes.title: Match
nodes.summary: Selecting a block by matching a value against constant, wildcard, binding, list, mapping and error patterns, with guards, narrowing and exhaustiveness.

must_cover.text: Write `match target { pattern => { ... } }`, where the target may be an expression or an action, clauses are tried in order and only the first clause whose pattern matches (and whose guard is true) runs
Match constant patterns such as `0`, `"GET"`, `true`, `()` and references to named constants, which match when DeepEquals (the `==` relation) holds and bind no variables
Combine patterns with `|` in one clause, as in `1|2|3 => { ... }`, knowing every alternative must bind the same set of variables
Use `_` as a catch-all clause, knowing the wildcard match pattern matches any value except an error

Capture parts of the value with `var x`, `var [a, b]` or `var {name}`, distinguishing identifiers under `var` (new variables) from bare identifiers (constant references), and keeping patterns linear (no variable bound twice)
Use list match patterns such as `[1, var x]` and `[var first, ...var rest]` to match on list length and members
Use mapping match patterns such as `{kind: "circle", radius: var r}` (optionally with `...var rest`), which match when every listed field matches, regardless of other fields
Use error match patterns such as `error(var msg)`, `error(var msg, var cause)` and `error MyError(var msg, code = var c)` to match an error's message, cause, detail fields and error type
Add a match guard with `pattern if cond => { ... }`, where `cond` is boolean, sees the pattern's variables, and a false guard moves on to the next clause

Know a match guard may contain a function or method call only if the match target's static type is readonly, or the callee is isolated and every argument (and the receiver object) has a readonly static type

Explain that a value matches a pattern when it looks like the pattern's type, so a mutable value can match without belonging to that type, while an error match pattern with a type reference requires the error to belong to the referenced error type

Rely on narrowing: when the match target is a variable, its type within a clause's guard and block is narrowed to the target type read-only-intersected with the clause's pattern type minus the patterns of preceding unguarded clauses
Know that a clause whose patterns cannot match, given the target's static type and the preceding unguarded clauses, has unreachable statements and is therefore a compile-time error

Explain exhaustiveness: a match is exhaustive when the target's static type is covered by the patterns of unguarded clauses (a clause without a guard or with a singleton `true` guard), and an exhaustive match completes normally only if one of its blocks can

out_of_scope: on fail clauses on match statements (concept.error_handling)

nodes.title: Modules
nodes.summary: How Ballerina programs are divided into modules and packages, and how a module part imports and refers to other modules.

must_cover.text: Explain that a module's source form is an ordered collection of one or more source parts (UTF-8 encoded), each matching `module-part`, where import declarations must come before all other declarations and the remaining top-level declarations may appear in any order

Identify a module by an organization name and a module name made of one or more dot-separated parts, both restricted to `RestrictedIdentifier` (an ASCII letter followed by ASCII letters and digits, with each underscore followed by a letter or digit), and know organization names starting with `ballerina` are reserved for the platform

Explain that the platform combines modules into a package whose name is the first part of each module name, that binary packages live in repositories organized by organization, package name and SemVer version, and that a package's `Ballerina.toml` controls the versions used for referenced modules
Explain that a package controls which of its modules are exported, and that a module that is not exported is visible only to modules within the same package
Explain that each source module can be compiled separately into a binary module and that compiling it needs only the binary form of the modules it references
Write import declarations such as `import ballerina/http;` and `import myorg/util.strings as str;`, knowing the organization name defaults to the importing module's organization when omitted
Use `import org/mod as _;` to include a module in the program and run its initialization without binding a module prefix
Explain that it is a compile error for a source part to import a module with a module prefix and then never use that prefix
Explain that a module must not directly or indirectly import itself: the directed graph of module imports must be acyclic

Refer to another module's public declarations with a qualified identifier `prefix:name`, with no white space allowed before or after the colon (`NoSpaceColon`), where the prefix must be declared by an import declaration in the same source part
Mark module-level declarations `public` so they can be referenced from other modules; without `public` a module-scope identifier can be referenced only within its own module

Explain that module prefixes declared by imports are in the same prefix symbol space as XML namespace prefixes declared by `xmlns`, that this symbol space is distinct from the module's main symbol space, and that it belongs to a source part rather than to the whole module

Use the predeclared prefixes `boolean`, `decimal`, `error`, `float`, `function`, `future`, `int`, `map`, `object`, `stream`, `string`, `table`, `transaction`, `typedesc` and `xml` to refer to the matching `lang.*` module without an import (e.g. `int:MAX_VALUE`, `string:Char`), and know an import that uses one of these prefixes overrides the predeclaration

out_of_scope: Module initialization order and the module init function (concept.program_execution)
Lexical rules for identifiers and quoted identifiers (concept.lexical_structure)
Package manifest and CLI details, which the spec leaves to the Ballerina platform
nodes.notes: The spec does not state the default module prefix when `as` is omitted; no item claims one. Package layout, Ballerina.toml contents and repositories are platform-defined and only mentioned at the level of detail in section 3.

nodes.title: Immutability
nodes.summary: How values and variables can be mutated, the deep read-only bit, inherent types of structured values, and describing and constructing immutable values with `readonly`.

must_cover.text: Explain that both variables and values can be mutated, that only values with storage identity can be mutated, and that a mutation is visible through every reference to the value

Distinguish a value that looks like a type (its current shape is in the type) from one that belongs to it (it will keep looking like the type however it is mutated), and know a variable only ever holds values that belong to its declared type
Explain the read-only bit, which is fixed when a value is constructed and makes immutability deep, so everything reachable from a read-only value is also read-only
Classify basic types as inherently immutable (nil, boolean, int, float, decimal, string, error, function, typedesc, handle) or selectively immutable (xml, list, mapping, table, object)
Explain that a `final` variable cannot be reassigned after initialization but may still hold a mutable value, so finality is not deep
Use the `readonly` type, which contains exactly the values whose read-only bit is on, and `readonly & T` to describe immutable values of type T

Explain that shapes have a primary aspect and a read-only aspect, that every type descriptor except `readonly` ignores the read-only aspect, and that equal plain data values may differ only in read-only bits

Explain that a mutable structured value carries an inherent type and the runtime rejects (with a panic) any mutation that would give it a shape outside that type, so it belongs to a type exactly when its inherent type is a subtype
Explain that an immutable structured value's inherent type is the singleton type of its shape, so it belongs to any type that contains its shape
Construct immutable values by giving constructors a readonly contextually expected type (e.g. `readonly & int[] xs = [1, 2];`), by casting with `<readonly>`, or by calling `cloneReadOnly()`
Explain that storing into or removing a member of an immutable structured value compiles but panics at runtime, because the static type does not guarantee the value is mutable

Explain mapping field read-only bits, that a field declared `readonly` cannot be assigned or removed and its value is read-only, and that a closed record whose fields are all `readonly` is a subtype of `readonly`
Explain that each selectively immutable basic type splits into a read-only and a mutable uniform type, and mutation can never move a value between them

out_of_scope: Readonly classes and readonly objects (concept.classes, concept.objects)
nodes.notes: 5.6.5 lists string among inherently immutable types under 'all simple types' though string is a sequence type; xml:Text is also inherently immutable (5.3.2).

nodes.title: Numeric types
nodes.summary: The int, float and decimal basic types, the byte type and built-in int subtypes, numeric literal syntax and typing, and explicit numeric conversion.

must_cover.text: Use the `int` type for 64-bit two's complement signed integers from -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807, available as `int:MIN_VALUE` and `int:MAX_VALUE`
Write int literals in decimal (no leading zeros except `0`) or hexadecimal with a `0x`/`0X` prefix such as `0xFF`
Use `byte` for ints in the range 0 to 255 inclusive, and know it is equivalent to the built-in subtype `int:Unsigned8`

Use the built-in int subtypes `int:Signed8`, `int:Signed16`, `int:Signed32`, `int:Unsigned8`, `int:Unsigned16` and `int:Unsigned32` and their range constants such as `int:SIGNED32_MAX_VALUE` and `int:UNSIGNED16_MAX_VALUE`

Use `float` for IEEE 754-2008 64-bit binary floating point, knowing all NaN bit patterns are the same value, +0.0 and -0.0 are distinct values with the same shape, operations round ties to even and no extended precision is used for intermediate results
Write floating point literals with a fraction or exponent (`1.5`, `.5`, `2e10`, `1.0E-3`), hexadecimal floating point literals such as `0x1.8p1`, and the `f`/`F` suffix to force float
Use `decimal` for IEEE 754-2008 decimal128-subset values with a 34-digit coefficient, knowing it has no NaN, infinities, subnormals or negative zero and that operations which would produce them panic
Write decimal literals with the `d`/`D` suffix such as `1.20d`, and explain that decimal shape is the mathematical value so `1.0d` and `1.00d` have the same shape despite different precision

Determine the type of a numeric literal: a `f` suffix or hex float literal gives float, a `d` suffix gives decimal, a literal with fraction or exponent may be float or decimal, otherwise int, float or decimal; candidates disjoint from the contextually expected type are dropped and the first of int, float, decimal remaining is chosen (so `decimal d = 1.5;` is a decimal)
Explain that a numeric literal's precise type is a singleton type containing its value and its broad type is the containing basic type
Explain that Ballerina never converts implicitly between numeric types, so mixing int and float requires an explicit conversion such as `<float>i`

Convert between numeric types with a type cast, following NumericConvert: int to float or decimal keeps the mathematical value, float and decimal convert to the closest value, and conversion to int rounds and fails (making the cast panic) for NaN or out-of-range values
Use the `float:NaN`, `float:Infinity`, `float:PI` and `float:E` constants and test values with `float:isNaN`, `float:isInfinite` and `float:isFinite`

out_of_scope: Arithmetic, shift and bitwise operators and overflow behaviour (concept.arithmetic_operators)
Numeric comparison and equality, including NaN and -0.0 (concept.comparison_equality)
nodes.notes: In 5.8.4 the 'round, error for NaN or out of int range' cell spans both the float and decimal rows (rowspan), so it applies to float-to-int and decimal-to-int. The rounding mode used for conversion to int is not named in 5.8.4.

nodes.title: Objects
nodes.summary: Object values that combine fields and methods, described structurally by object type descriptors and created directly with object constructor expressions.

must_cover.text: Describe object types such as `type Shape object { public string name; public function area() returns float; };` listing field descriptors and method declarations
Explain that an object's fields and methods share one symbol space, so a field and a method cannot have the same name, and that there is no method overloading
Use `map`, `join` and `start` as method names even though they are normally reserved keywords, and know a method declaration in an object type cannot be named `init`
Create an object directly with an object constructor expression such as `var counter = object { int n = 0; function inc() { self.n += 1; } };`
Access an object's fields and methods inside method bodies through `self` (they are not implicitly in scope), knowing `self` is implicitly final
Call an object's methods with `obj.method(args)`, which builds the argument list as for a function call, knowing method-call syntax cannot invoke a remote method
Control member visibility with `public` (visible in all modules), `private` (visible only inside the method bodies of the object constructor or class) and the default module-level visibility

Explain that object types are inclusive and structural: an object belongs to a type if it has at least the described fields and methods with matching names, visibility, remote flag and types, so every object belongs to `object {}`
Explain that because visibility regions must match for subtyping, an object type with module-level-visibility members can have subtypes defined only in the same module

Include another object type's fields and method declarations with `*T;`, overriding an included member only with a subtype, knowing a field cannot override a method (or vice versa) and an object type cannot directly or indirectly include itself
Explain that it is an error for two inclusions to bring in same-named fields, or same-named methods with different signatures, unless the including type overrides them

Explain that an included type must be an object type, a distinct or intersection object type, or a class with no `private` members and no `readonly` qualifier, and that including a type with an `isolated`, `client` or `service` qualifier requires the including type to have that qualifier too

Describe read-only objects with `readonly & object { ... }`, since an object type descriptor alone does not constrain the read-only bit, and know a read-only object's field values are read-only and cannot be changed after construction

Declare object constructor fields with optional `final` and an initializer, knowing a field without an initializer must be initialized by an `init` method, a `final` field must be assigned exactly once, and an `init` method in an object constructor must have no parameters

Explain that an object constructor builds a read-only object when every field is `final` with a type that is a subtype of `readonly`, or when the applicable contextually expected type (or the referenced type) is a subtype of `readonly`

Write `object T { ... }` to include type `T` in an object constructor so the object gets `T`'s type-ids; without a type reference the applicable contextually expected type must be definite and supplies the type-ids
Explain that annotations on an object constructor and its members are evaluated each time it is evaluated, so every object it creates has its own type descriptor

out_of_scope: Remote methods and client objects (concept.client_objects); resource methods (concept.resource_methods)
Isolated objects and lock requirements on self (concept.isolation, concept.lock_statement)
nodes.notes: 5.5.3.7 says a subtype T' needs, for each member f of T, a corresponding member f' 'of T' (the text says 'of T', which reads as a typo for T').

nodes.title: Program execution
nodes.summary: How a Ballerina program made of a root module and its imports runs through an initialization phase and a listening phase, including the module init function.

must_cover.text: Explain that a program consists of a distinguished root module plus every module it imports directly or indirectly, determined at compile time from the root module
Describe program execution as two consecutive phases, an initialization phase followed by a listening phase, and that execution terminates either successfully or unsuccessfully with an error value
Explain that a module is initialized only after all the modules it depends on, and that otherwise modules are initialized in the order they are imported

Explain that the compiler synthesizes an initialization function for each module that evaluates the expressions initializing its module-level declarations and returns the associated error if any evaluation completes abruptly
Explain that if any module's initialization fails, program execution immediately terminates unsuccessfully with the error returned by that module's initialization function

Define a module-level `function init() returns error? { ... }`, which is called automatically at the end of the module's initialization; it must not be `public`, must take no parameters, and its return type must be a subtype of `error?` that contains `()`

Explain that if the module `init` function returns an error or terminates abruptly, the module's initialization fails, and that the root module's `init` function is the last function called in the initialization phase

Explain that the spec defines no mechanism for command-line arguments: the platform generates a command-line processing module, which becomes the new root module, parses the arguments according to the parameter types, annotations and names of the original root module's public functions, and calls one of them (typically `main`)
Explain that execution proceeds to the listening phase only if the initialization phase succeeds, and that if there are then no module listeners the program terminates gracefully

out_of_scope: Configurable variables and the configuration check (concept.configurable)
Listener lifecycle in the listening phase (concept.services_listeners)
Module variables that must be initialized in init (concept.variables)
Command-line argument syntax and `main` conventions, which are platform-defined
nodes.notes: The spec only says the generated command-line module calls 'a public function of the specified root module (typically the main function)'; main-function rules are not specified by 2024R1.

nodes.title: Query expressions
nodes.summary: Language-integrated, SQL-like queries built from from, where, let, limit, order by and select clauses that produce lists, maps, tables, strings, xml or streams, plus query actions with a do clause.

must_cover.text: Write query expressions such as `from var p in people where p.age > 18 select p.name`, and explain them as a pipeline of clauses transforming a sequence of frames (variable bindings)
Use `from` with a typed binding pattern or `var` over any iterable value, and use several `from` clauses to iterate over every combination of their values
Filter frames with `where`, whose boolean condition also narrows variable types for all following clauses
Add computed bindings with `let int total = p.price * p.qty`, where a let clause with several declarations behaves like consecutive let clauses
Use `select expr` to emit one value per frame, which becomes a member of the constructed result

Construct lists, maps (with `map from ... select [key, value]`), keyed tables (`table key(id) from ...`), strings (concatenating string results), xml (concatenating xml results) and streams from a query

Explain how the result basic type is chosen: an explicit `map`, `table key(...)` or `stream` keyword first, then the applicable contextually expected type, then the basic type of the first `in` expression (which must be a list, table, string, stream or xml), so a query over a stream yields a stream without the `stream` keyword
Explain that queries constructing streams run lazily, with clauses executed as `next` is called, while all other queries run eagerly during evaluation

Explain that when an iterator in `from` returns an error, the query stops and that error becomes the result (eager), or is returned by the stream `next` call (lazy), where check-failures are also returned and panics still panic
Limit the number of frames with `limit n`, where `n` is an `int` evaluated without the frame bindings and a negative value panics
Sort frames with `order by e1 ascending, e2 descending` (ascending by default), where keys must be of ordered types, the sort is stable, and both `()` and NaN sort to the end in either direction
Explain that a query building a list, mapping, table or xml value constructs a read-only value when the applicable expected type is a subtype of `readonly`
Explain that variables bound by query clauses are implicitly final and cannot be assigned
Use a query action `from var x in xs where ... do { ... }` to run a statement block for each frame, which evaluates to nil, or to an error if a clause completes early with an error
Use actions such as client remote method calls inside query clauses (the `in` expression of from and join, let, select and collect), which makes the whole query an action
Explain that clause keywords marked not-reserved in the grammar (such as `where`, `select`, `limit`, `order`, `by`, `join`, `outer`, `group`, `collect`, `conflict`) can still be used as identifiers

out_of_scope: join, group by, collect, aggregated variables and on conflict (concept.query_joins_grouping)
nodes.notes: 2024R1 (B.1) allows a query-select-expr to construct a stream without the `stream` keyword. 6.35.10 says a mapping-constructing query must specify `map`. Order-by stability follows from the index tie-break in the CompareKL definition.

nodes.title: Joins and grouping
nodes.summary: Inner and outer equijoins, group by with aggregated variables, collect for whole-query aggregation, langlib aggregation calls, and on conflict handling for maps and tables built by queries.

must_cover.text: Join two sources with `join var d in depts on e.deptId equals d.id`, an inner equijoin that compares keys with DeepEquals
Explain join scoping: the `in` expression sees neither earlier nor join variables, the left side of `equals` sees only earlier variables and the right side sees only the join variables
Use `outer join var d in depts on ...` for a left outer join, which must use `var`, gives join variables type `T?`, and binds them to `()` when there is no match
Group frames with `group by deptId`, which partitions frames by DeepEquals of the grouping keys and emits one frame per group in the order each group first appears
Declare grouping keys inline with `group by var k = expr`, which is equivalent to a `let` clause followed by `group by k`
Explain that after `group by` each non-key variable becomes an aggregated variable of type `[T, T...]`, and after `collect` every variable becomes one of type `T[]`
Reference an aggregated variable only where a spread is allowed, as a list constructor member (`[price]`, the same as `[...price]`) or a function rest argument (`sum(price)`)

Aggregate with unqualified calls such as `sum(price)`, `avg(x)`, `max(x)`, `min(x)`, `count(x)`, `first(x)` and `last(x)`, which resolve to the lang module of the member basic type (e.g. `int:sum`) or else `lang.value`, and give `()` for an empty list when the function needs at least one argument

Use a query-collect expression `from var o in orders collect sum(o.amount)` to aggregate every frame into one value, where the collect expression gets the query expected type and an early iterator error becomes the result
Combine `group by` with `select` to emit one result per group, e.g. `group by cat select {cat, total: sum(price)}`
Explain that when a query builds a map or keyed table, a new member with an existing key replaces the old one in the same position unless an `on conflict` clause is given

Use `on conflict expr`, allowed only when building a keyed table or a map, whose `error?` result is evaluated on each key clash, with an error becoming the query result and nil letting the replacement go ahead

out_of_scope: Basic query clauses and result kinds (concept.query_expressions)
Per-function semantics of int/float/decimal aggregation functions (concept.langlib_numeric)
nodes.notes: 6.35.4 notes an optional optimisation when the join source is a table keyed by the equals expression; that is an implementation detail and is not covered. 6.35.11 wording 'the earlier new value replaces the earlier conflicting value' is garbled but intends that the new value replaces the old.

nodes.title: Raw templates
nodes.summary: Backtick strings with interpolations that, used without a tag, construct `object:RawTemplate` values holding the literal string parts and the interpolated values separately.

must_cover.text: Write backtick strings with `${expr}` interpolations, knowing that every other character, including a `$` not followed by `{`, is literal
Write an untagged template such as `` `SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ${id}` `` to construct a raw template object instead of a string
Describe `object:RawTemplate`, a distinct object type with fields `public (readonly & string[]) strings` and `public (any|error)[] insertions`
Explain that `insertions` holds the interpolated values evaluated in order and `strings` holds the literal text split at the interpolation points, so `strings` has one more member than `insertions`
Explain that each raw template expression has its own class (a subtype of RawTemplate) whose `strings` value is created once, while a new `insertions` list is created on every evaluation

Explain that the type of `insertions` comes from the contextually expected type (or the interpolation types), as for a list constructor, and that the fields are read-only if the expected type requires it
Use a subtype of `object:RawTemplate` with a narrower `insertions` type as the expected type, so that the compiler checks the types of the interpolated expressions

nodes.notes: constrained_raw_templates is a direct consequence of the 6.6.4 rule that the insertions type follows the contextually expected type; the spec gives no example.

nodes.title: Records
nodes.summary: Record type descriptors that give each named field its own type, with required, optional, defaulted and readonly fields, open or closed shapes, rest descriptors and type inclusion.

must_cover.text: Define record types such as `type Person record { string name; int age; };` whose fields are required, and create values of them with mapping constructors
Declare optional fields with `T f?;`, meaning the field may be absent but if present its value must belong to `T`
Declare fields with default values `int retries = 3;`, and explain the default is a closure evaluated each time a value is constructed without that field and does not affect the type
Explain that a field default-expression must meet the requirements for an isolated function and that it is a compile-time error for it to contain `check`
Explain that a mapping constructor adds default values for missing fields only after all specific and spread fields have been added

Distinguish inclusive records `record { ... }`, which also allow extra `anydata` fields (equivalent to `record {| ...; anydata...; |}`), from exclusive records `record {| ... |}`, which allow only the described fields
Use a record rest descriptor `record {| string name; int...; |}` to allow extra fields of a given type, and classify a record type as open (inclusive, or exclusive with rest) or closed
Declare `readonly` fields, whose read-only bit must be set and whose type is the intersection of `readonly` and the declared type
Explain that a closed record type in which every field is `readonly` is a subtype of `readonly`
Include the fields and rest descriptor of another record type with `*OtherRecord;`, and know a record may not directly or indirectly include itself

Override an included field with a field of the same name whose type is a subtype, and explain the error when two inclusions bring a same-named field or different rest descriptors that the including type does not override
Explain that in a mapping constructor whose inherent type is a record, a field written with a plain field name (not a string literal) must be declared in the record type
Explain that the order of field descriptors is not significant and that quoted identifiers let a field name be any non-empty string
Explain that for `R & readonly`, a field default whose result belongs to `Cloneable` gets ImmutableClone applied to it, and otherwise the field has no default

out_of_scope: map<T> types and mapping constructor syntax in general (concept.maps)
nodes.notes: Field descriptor grammar: `metadata [readonly] type-descriptor field-name [? | (= default-expression)] ;` — a field cannot be both optional and defaulted.

nodes.title: Regular expressions
nodes.summary: The `re` tagged data type for regular expressions (a preview feature in 2024R1), with its template syntax, supported Perl/ECMAScript-subset grammar, flags and semantics.

must_cover.text: Explain tagged data values: each data tag has its own basic type whose values are plain data, immutable and without storage identity, and in 2024R1 the only data tag is `re`, backed by `lang.regexp`
Recognise that regular expressions and `lang.regexp` have preview status in the 2024R1 specification
Write regular expressions as `re `[a-z]+\d*``, which are parsed at compile time (a syntax error is a compile-time error) so evaluating them cannot fail
Interpolate other regular expressions with `${r}`, which must have type `regexp:RegExp` and behaves as if `(?:r)` were inserted at that point
Use the type `regexp:RegExp` (also `string:RegExp`), which is part of `anydata` and has filler value `re```
Use literal characters, `.`, character classes `[a-z]` and `[^...]`, the escapes `\d \D \s \S \w \W`, `\r \n \t`, `\u{...}`, and backslash-quoted syntax characters such as `\.` and `\(`
Use quantifiers `*`, `+`, `?`, `{n}`, `{n,}` and `{n,m}`, and make them non-greedy with a trailing `?`
Use alternation `a|b`, capturing groups `( )`, non-capturing groups `(?: )` and the assertions `^` and `$`

Set flags inside a group with `(?i:...)` or `(?m-s:...)`, using flags `m` (multiline), `s` (dot-all), `i` (ignore case) and `x` (ignore white space outside character sets, with `#` comments), each at most once
Match Unicode properties with `\p{L}`, `\p{gc=Lu}`, `\p{sc=Latin}` and their negation `\P{...}` (general category `Cs` is not supported)
Explain that matching follows ECMAScript 2022 Unicode-mode semantics with Unicode 10, except that `.` matches any character other than 0xA and 0xD and `\s` matches Ballerina white space characters
Apply regular expressions with `lang.regexp` functions such as `find`, `isFullMatch` and `replaceAll`, and with `string` functions `matches` and `includesMatch`

out_of_scope: Lookahead/lookbehind and backreferences, which the 2024R1 RegExp grammar does not include
nodes.notes: Grammar: ReAtom `( [? ReFlagsOnOff :] ReDisjunction )` — `(?:...)` is the empty-flags case. 10.1 refers to `fullMatchGroup` but the lang.regexp module defines `fullMatchGroups`.

nodes.title: Resource methods
nodes.summary: Resource methods of client and service objects, identified by a method name and a resource path of names, path parameters and rest parameters.

must_cover.text: Declare resource methods such as `resource function get users/[string id]() returns User|error`, allowed only in client or service objects, where a resource method is identified by its method name together with its resource path
Write resource paths from segment names, path parameters `[T name]`, an optional final rest parameter `[T... name]`, or `.` for the empty path

Explain that path segments may be any `anydata` value (most commonly strings) and that a resource path maps to a tuple type: segment names to singleton strings, path parameters to their types, a rest parameter to a rest descriptor, and `.` to `[]`
Use the method name `get` for a resource method that just fetches the resource, knowing that for service objects the listener decides which method names are supported but should always support `get`
Know it is a compile error for an object to declare two resource methods with the same method name whose paths map to the same tuple type

Apply the divergence rule: if two resource methods with overlapping applicable method names diverge at some path position, it is a compile error unless at least one of them has a segment name (singleton string) at that position
Explain that segment names take priority over path parameters: a path parameter's type is narrowed to exclude the singleton strings that diverging resource methods declare at the same position
Use path parameters in the method body: a segment parameter is bound to the path value at its position and a rest parameter to a list of all values from its position onwards
Explain the resource access operation: given a method name, a list of path values and an argument list, it looks up the matching resource method, binds the path parameters and invokes the function

Explain resource delegation: a `get` resource whose return type includes a service object type delegates longer paths to the returned service, so that return type may only allow service objects and errors, its path must not end with a rest parameter, and no other resource path may have it as a prefix
Know that a resource method's return type must not allow function values or client object types

out_of_scope: Calling client resources with resource access actions (concept.client_objects)
nodes.notes: The applicable-method-name rule (only `get` at non-final positions; `get` plus m at a rest position) is only used to define divergence and is folded into divergence_rule.

nodes.title: Retry
nodes.summary: Re-executing a failing block with the retry statement, controlled by a RetryManager class such as error:DefaultRetryManager.

must_cover.text: Use `retry { ... }` to re-execute a block that fails through `check` or `fail`, with `error:DefaultRetryManager` deciding whether to retry when no manager type is given
Trace retry execution: create the manager with `new T(A)`, run the block, and on failure with error e call `shouldRetry(e)`, repeating if it returns true and otherwise continuing with the failure

Explain `error:DefaultRetryManager`: its `init(int count = 3)` sets the retry budget, and `shouldRetry` returns true (decrementing the count) only when the error is an `error:Retriable` and the count is still positive
Make errors retryable by the default manager by giving them a type that is a subtype of the distinct type `error:Retriable`
Select a manager class with `retry<MyRetryManager>(args) { ... }`, where the arguments go to the class's `init` and can be omitted when `init` has no required parameters
Implement a RetryManager class with `public function shouldRetry(E e) returns boolean`, where the parameter type E must be a supertype of the block's failure type
Explain that `RetryManager<E>` is contravariant in E: `RetryManager<E>` is a subtype of `RetryManager<E'>` if and only if E' is a subtype of E
Attach an `on fail` clause to a `retry` statement (new in 2024R1) to handle the failure that remains once retrying stops
Know that retry reacts only to failures (check-fail and `fail`), not to panics, which terminate the worker

nodes.title: Services and listeners
nodes.summary: Listener objects that receive network messages and dispatch them to attached service objects, declared with listener and service declarations and managed during the listening phase.

must_cover.text: Describe the `Listener<T,A>` object type, with methods `attach(T svc, A attachPoint)`, `detach(T svc)`, `start()`, `gracefulStop()` and `immediateStop()`, each returning `error?`, where `T` is a subtype of `service object {}` and `A` a subtype of `string[]|string|()`
Distinguish `gracefulStop` (finish handling messages already started, waiting for strands the listener created) from `immediateStop` (do not complete in-progress handling, cancelling those strands)

Declare a module listener with `listener MyListener ep = new (8080);`, which behaves like a final module variable that is also registered with the module; an error result or abrupt evaluation of its expression makes module initialization fail

Explain that a listener declaration's expression must have a static type equivalent to `L|E`, where `L` is a listener object type and `E` an error subtype (possibly `never`), and that without an explicit type descriptor the variable's type is `L`

Declare a service with `service /hello on ep { resource function get greeting() returns string { return "hi"; } }`, which constructs a service object and attaches it to each listener in its expression list
Explain the attach point passed as the second argument to `attach`: nil when absent, a string for a string literal, and an array of segment strings for an absolute resource path such as `/api/v1`

Attach one service to several listeners with `service on ep1, ep2 { ... }` or to a listener constructed inline, knowing each listener expression is registered as a module listener (registering the same object twice is the same as once) and a failing `attach` makes module initialization fail

Explain that the service object's type is the declared type descriptor if present, otherwise the union of the `T` inferred from each listener's `Listener<T,A>` type, and that `isolated service` is equivalent to an isolated object constructor

Implement service objects with remote and resource methods that are invoked by a listener object from a library module, knowing Ballerina does not yet provide a way to implement such listeners entirely in Ballerina

Use a service method's return value to tell the listener how to proceed: an error for a failure, a service object to handle the message further, nil when no further handling is needed, or a response value (a stream can model multiple responses)
Explain that a listener can pass a client object to a service method so the method sends responses by calling the client's remote methods, avoiding the limits of returning a response value

Explain the listening phase: with no module listeners the program terminates gracefully; otherwise each module listener's `start` is called (an error ends the program unsuccessfully), and the phase continues until the program exits or a graceful or immediate stop request calls `gracefulStop` or `immediateStop` on every registered listener
Register shutdown handlers with `runtime:onGracefulStop(handler)`, which are called during graceful termination in reverse order of registration

Register and deregister listeners at runtime with `runtime:registerListener(l)` and `runtime:deregisterListener(l)`, where `l` belongs to `runtime:DynamicListener` (`start`, `gracefulStop`, `immediateStop`)

Explain that a listener may use the isolated bit of a service object and of its remote methods to decide whether concurrent calls are safe, and that the compiler may infer `isolated` for services that are not explicitly declared isolated

out_of_scope: Protocol-specific listeners such as http:Listener, which belong to the standard library

nodes.title: Workers
nodes.summary: Ballerina's concurrency model of threads and cooperatively scheduled strands, the default and named workers of a function, and the fork statement.

must_cover.text: Explain the concurrency model: a program runs on one or more threads, each divided into strands that are cooperatively multitasked like coroutines, so two strands of the same thread never run at the same time

Identify what makes a strand yield: receive actions, wait actions, flush actions, sync send actions, `runtime:sleep`, and external functions that block; other langlib functions do not yield by themselves

Know that only named worker declarations and `start` create new strands, which stay on the current thread unless the spec allows otherwise (named workers and fork in an isolated function, or an isolated start)
Declare named workers in a function body with `worker w returns T { ... }` (return type defaulting to `()`), each running on its own new strand
Explain the default worker: the function's unnamed worker runs on the caller's strand, its termination value becomes the function's return value, and a panic in it makes the call panic

Explain that with named workers a function body runs in three stages: statements before the worker declarations, then all named workers start, then the remaining default-worker statements run without waiting for the workers
Know that parameters and variables declared before the worker declarations are visible inside named workers, while variables declared after them in the default worker are not
Use a worker name as a variable reference to get a `future<T>` for its return value, and know it is a compile error if that name could be evaluated more than once in one execution
Know that when a function's default worker terminates the function returns without waiting for, or terminating, its named workers

Distinguish normal termination (with success, or with failure when the termination value is an error) from abnormal termination caused by a panic, and know that falling off the end of a worker returns `()`
Use `fork { worker a { ... } worker b { ... } }` to start workers that run in parallel on new strands, see in-scope variables, and whose names can be referenced after the fork statement
Know that workers created by a fork statement are peers of each other but not of the function's default worker or its named workers
Declare `transactional worker w { ... }` only in the body of a `transactional` function; such a worker is a transactional scope

out_of_scope: Isolation rules that allow parallel threads (concept.isolation)

nodes.title: Streams
nodes.summary: Lazily generated sequences of values with a completion value, described by stream<T,C>, constructed with new from a StreamImplementor or by queries, and processed with lang.stream functions.

must_cover.text: Declare stream types `stream<T,C>` and `stream<T>` (same as `stream<T,()>`), and explain that a completion type `C` without nil describes an unbounded stream
Explain the two primitive stream operations: `next`, which behaves like Iterator `next`, and `close`, which returns `C?`, is idempotent and runs automatically when generation completes
Construct streams with `new stream<T,E>(impl)` wrapping a StreamImplementor object, or an empty stream with `new stream<T>()` (or an implicit `new`), whose `next` returns nil
Implement a StreamImplementor with `public isolated function next() returns record {| T value; |}|C` and optionally `public isolated function close() returns C?`
Explain that calling `next` after `close` on a StreamImplementor must panic, and that a missing `close` method behaves like one that puts the object in a closed state and returns `()`
Explain that a stream does not keep the values it has produced, so a second iteration over the same stream yields an empty sequence
Explain that `foreach` requires an iterable whose completion type is nil, so a `stream<T, error?>` must be consumed with `next()`, `forEach` or a query instead
Use `lang.stream` functions `next`, `close`, `iterator`, `map`, `filter`, `forEach` (returns the completion value) and `reduce` (returns the result or the stream error)
Turn an array into a stream with `arr.toStream()`
Create streams with query expressions (`stream from ...`, or a query whose expected type or source is a stream), whose clauses run lazily as `next` is called
Explain that `stream<T,C>` works like a class with `new` even though it is not a class, because Ballerina does not yet support parameterized classes

nodes.notes: 5.5.7 says the stream type 'works like a class' but 6.8.2 class-descriptor explicitly allows stream-type-descriptor in new.

nodes.title: String conversion
nodes.summary: The ToString operation in its expression, informal and direct styles, the `toString`, `toBalString` and `fromBalString` functions, and numeric and boolean parsing and formatting functions.

must_cover.text: Distinguish the three ToString styles: expression style (looks like a Ballerina expression), informal style (similar but avoids Ballerina-specific syntax) and direct style (converts the value itself, e.g. a string stays unchanged and xml becomes XML text)

Use `v.toString()` (`value:toString`) for a direct-style conversion of any non-error value, e.g. `"xyz".toString()` is `xyz`, `1.20d.toString()` is `1.20`, and nested members of lists and maps use informal style such as `[1,"a"]`
Use `v.toBalString()` for expression style, which for acyclic anydata produces valid Ballerina source that evaluates to a value `==` to v (e.g. `"xyz"` with quotes, `1.20d`, `float:NaN`, `()`)
Use `value:fromBalString(s)` to parse the subset of expression syntax produced by `toBalString` back into an anydata value, returning an error if it cannot be parsed

Know how special values are rendered, namely nil as `()` in expression style and `null` in informal style, float NaN and infinity as `float:NaN`/`float:Infinity` in expression style and `NaN`/`Infinity` otherwise, and decimals with a `d` suffix only in expression style
Know the rendering of structured values, namely arrays as `[X,Y]`, maps as `{"x":X,"y":Y}` and tables as `table key(k) [R1,R2]` in expression style or `[R1,R2]` otherwise
Convert errors with `e.toString()` and `e.toBalString()`, which render `error D1&D2 (M,C,F1=V1,...)` with type-ids, message, cause and detail fields
Explain that an object with a `toString` method is converted using that method's result, while an object without one is rendered as `object` with its type-ids and a unique identifier
Explain that ToString detects cycles and renders them as `...[N]` in expression style (N the 0-based depth index) and `...` otherwise

Parse strings with `int:fromString`, `int:fromHexString`, `float:fromString` (accepting `NaN` and `Infinity`), `float:fromHexString`, `decimal:fromString` and `boolean:fromString`, each returning an error on invalid input

Format numbers with `int:toHexString`, `float:toHexString`, `float:toFixedString(x, digits)` and `float:toExpString(x, digits)`, knowing the last two panic for negative fractionDigits and round ties to even

nodes.notes: In the ToString table the direct-style cell for nil is empty in the HTML; it is unclear whether direct style renders nil as an empty string or falls back to informal `null`. Left out of items.

nodes.title: Strings
nodes.summary: The immutable string sequence type of Unicode scalar values, string literals and escapes, indexing, iteration, concatenation and string template expressions.

must_cover.text: Explain that a string is a sequence of zero or more Unicode scalar values (code points 0x0 to 0x10FFFF excluding surrogates), may contain noncharacters such as 0xFFFE, and is inherently immutable with no storage identity
Write double-quoted string literals that cannot contain raw newlines, using the escapes `\t`, `\n`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"` and numeric escapes `\u{1F600}`

Explain sequence semantics for strings, that a single character is itself a string of length 1 (a singleton), concatenating with the empty string gives the same value, and this differs from lists whose members are separate values
Use the built-in subtype `string:Char` for strings of length 1
Index a string with `s[i]` to get a `string:Char`, knowing it panics when `i < 0` or `i >= s.length()`
Iterate over a string with `foreach`, which yields each character as a `string:Char` in order with nil completion
Concatenate strings with `+`, whose static type is `string` modified by singleton typing when both operands are constant
Build strings with string templates ``string `Hello ${name}!` ``, where each interpolation `${expr}` must have static type that is a subtype of `boolean|int|float|decimal|string`
Explain that string template interpolations are evaluated left to right and each result is converted with the direct-style ToString, so `string `${1.0}`` gives "1.0"
Explain that every character in a BacktickString outside `${...}` is literal (no escape sequences), and include a literal backtick with the interpolation `${"`"}`
Compare strings with `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, which order lexicographically by Unicode code point
Call `lang.string` functions with method-call syntax, such as `s.length()`, `s.substring(0, 3)`, `s.indexOf("x")`, `s.trim()` and `s.toUpperAscii()`

out_of_scope: XML, raw and regular-expression templates (concept.xml, concept.raw_templates, concept.regexp)
nodes.notes: String literal grammar has only double-quoted literals; there is no separate multi-line string literal form in 2024R1.

nodes.title: Tables
nodes.summary: Ordered collections of mapping values accessed by a key derived from read-only fields, described by table types with key constraints and built with table constructors and lang.table functions.

must_cover.text: Declare table types `table<R>`, whose row type must be a subtype of `map<any|error>`, and explain that a table keeps rows in order but gives no access by position
Declare keyed tables with `table<Employee> key(id)`, where each key field must be a required, `readonly` field of the row type with a subtype of `anydata`
Use multi-field keys `key(first, last)`, whose key value is a tuple of the field values, and look rows up with `t[k1, k2]` (equivalent to `t[[k1, k2]]`)
Use `table<R> key<K>` to constrain key values to type `K`, and know that a keyless table satisfies `key<never>`
Explain that key values must be unique, compared with DeepEquals, that this is enforced when the table is constructed and on every mutation, and that key field values must be acyclic plain data
Create keyless tables (empty key sequence) whose rows are not identified by a key
Construct tables with `table key(email) [{email: "a@x", name: "A"}, ...]`, where every row must give each key field as a constant expression and duplicate keys are a compile-time error

Explain that the key sequence comes from the constructor key-specifier or the expected type (both must agree if present), and that without an expected type the row type is the smallest record supertype of the rows, with an empty row list then being an error
Look up a row with `t[k]`, which returns `R?` and yields `()` when no row has key `k`
Explain that an assignment target cannot refer to a table member, so rows are added or replaced with `add` and `put`
