Use `t.add(row)`, which panics if a row with the same key exists, versus `t.put(row)`, which replaces the row with the same key in the same position and panics if the row is inconsistent with the inherent type
Use `t.get(k)` and `t.remove(k)` (both panic when no row has key `k`), `t.removeIfHasKey(k)`, `t.hasKey(k)`, `t.keys()` and `t.removeAll()`
Use `length`, `toArray`, `forEach`, `reduce`, `filter` (keeps the key type) and `map` (returns a `table<...> key<never>`) on tables
Use `t.nextKey()` on a `key<int>` table to get the maximum used key plus one, or 0 when no key is used
Iterate over table rows in order with `foreach`, with value type the row type and completion type nil
Build tables from query expressions with `table key(id) from var r in rows select r`

out_of_scope: On conflict handling when a query constructs a keyed table (concept.query_joins_grouping)
Join clause optimisation using tables (implementation detail)
nodes.notes: lang.table nextKey doc contains an unresolved 'XXX should it be 0, if the maximum used key value is < 0?' remark in the 2024R1 spec.

nodes.title: Transaction manager
nodes.summary: The abstract transaction manager behind Ballerina transactions, covering global transactions and branches, the per-strand transaction stack, and the Begin, Commit (two-phase commit) and Rollback operations.

must_cover.text: Explain global transactions: one or more transaction branches, each the work of a single strand, with each branch identified by an XID combining the global transaction id and a branch id
Explain that each strand has a transaction stack, that the strand is in transaction mode when the stack is non-empty, and that the top entry is its current transaction branch
Describe the Begin operation: it starts a global transaction, pushes its initiating branch onto the strand's stack, and optionally receives information about previous attempts in a retry sequence

Describe the Commit operation: it pops the branch and starts a commit, running two-phase commit (prepare, then decide) and deciding to roll back with a cause error if any participant cannot commit or does not respond

Explain that once the manager decides, it calls the registered commit handlers or rollback handlers (passing the rollback cause) for its branches, tells the participants, and Commit returns the rollback error or nil
Describe the Rollback operation: it pops the branch and calls the rollback handlers, passing them the given error or nil
Explain that for retry transactions Commit and Rollback receive the RetryManager, call its `shouldRetry`, record the result, and pass it to rollback handlers as `willRetry`

Explain cross-program transactions: transaction managers coordinate over a network protocol, listeners join service remote or resource methods to the global transaction (and do not call a `transactional` method unless they can), and transactional client remote methods propagate the transaction to the recipient
Know that the transaction manager may run in the same process or a separate one, but should not be connected to the program over an unreliable network

out_of_scope: Transaction statement syntax and lang.transaction functions (concept.transactions)
nodes.notes: 7.24.1.3 says the Rollback operation 'initiates a commit of the global transaction', which looks like a typo for 'rollback'; the item describes it as rollback.

nodes.title: Transactions
nodes.summary: Language support for transactions, covering the transaction statement, commit and rollback, transactional scope and functions, retry transaction, and the lang.transaction functions.

must_cover.text: Write `transaction { ...; check commit; }`, knowing the block must contain a `commit` action and the compiler must verify that every exit other than a panic or fail has executed `commit` or `rollback`

Use the `commit` action, whose result type is `transaction:Error?` (an error when the transaction manager decided to roll back) and which does not change control flow; it is allowed only lexically inside a transaction statement
Use `rollback;` or `rollback e;` inside a transaction statement to roll back explicitly, passing the optional error to rollback handlers, without changing control flow

Explain that if the transaction block fails or panics before commit or rollback, the transaction statement rolls back with that error and then continues the fail or panic (a panic in the block does not immediately terminate the worker)

Explain transactional scope: the part of a transaction block before commit or rollback, and the body of a `transactional` function; a `transactional` function can be called (including with `start`) only in a transactional scope

Declare `transactional` functions and remote or resource methods, and know a function type without `transactional` is a subtype of the same function type with `transactional` (the opposite direction from `isolated`)
Use the `transactional` expression to test at runtime whether the current strand is in transaction mode
Know that a transaction statement inside a transactional scope is a compile-time error, but running one while the strand is already in transaction mode begins a new, independent transaction

Use `retry transaction { ... }` (optionally `retry<M>(args) transaction { ... }`) to retry a transaction, which passes information about the previous attempt to Begin and does not retry if the transaction committed but the block failed afterwards
Attach an `on fail` clause to a transaction or retry transaction statement (new in 2024R1)

Register handlers with `transaction:onCommit(handler)` and `transaction:onRollback(handler)`, where a `CommitHandler` takes `Info` and a `RollbackHandler` takes `(Info info, error? cause, boolean willRetry)`
Know that in-memory Ballerina state is not transactional: rolling back does not restore variables or values, so undo such changes in rollback handlers

Use the transactional lang.transaction functions `transaction:info()`, `setRollbackOnly(e)`, `getRollbackOnly()`, `setData(d)` and `getData()`, and `transaction:getInfo(xid)` to look up a transaction by XID
Know that a `transactional` named worker, or `start` of a transactional function, creates a new transaction branch joined to the current global transaction

out_of_scope: Transaction manager Begin/Commit/Rollback operations and two-phase commit (concept.transaction_manager)

nodes.title: Type casts and tests
nodes.summary: The distinction between casting and conversion, the `<T>` type cast expression with numeric conversion, the `is`/`!is` type test, and the error-returning `ensureType`.

must_cover.text: Distinguish casting, which checks that a value belongs to another type without changing it, from conversion, which produces a possibly different value and never mutates its input; all conversions must be explicit
Write a type cast `<T> expr`, which returns the value unchanged if it belongs to T and otherwise panics

Use a type cast to convert between numeric types when T contains exactly one numeric basic type (e.g. `<int>3.7`, `<float>n`, `<decimal>f`), applying NumericConvert and panicking if the conversion fails (e.g. NaN or out-of-range to int)
Explain that the static type of `<T> e` is the intersection of T with e's static type (adjusted for possible numeric conversion)
Explain that casting a possibly-error expression to a type that excludes error is a compile error, and use `checkpanic` instead to assert an expression is not an error
Explain that the contextually expected type for the operand of a cast is the intersection of the cast's own expected type and T, so constructors inside the cast build values of T
Use `<readonly>` both to make constructors in the operand build immutable values and to verify at runtime that the result's read-only bit is on
Recognize a cast whose parameter is only annotations, such as `<@a> expr`, whose sole effect is to add annotations to the contextually expected type
Use `expr is T` and `expr !is T` to test at runtime whether a value belongs to a type, producing boolean
Use `value:ensureType(v, T)` (or `v.ensureType()` with an inferred typedesc) to cast safely, returning an error instead of panicking when the value does not belong to the type

out_of_scope: Structural conversion with cloneWithType / fromJsonWithType (concept.value_cloning, concept.json_anydata)
nodes.notes: 6.28 says the result of `is` is true if v belongs to the type; elsewhere (match patterns) 'looks like' is used, so a mutable value that merely looks like T does not satisfy `is T`.

nodes.title: Distinct types
nodes.summary: Distinct object and error types, which give nominal-style typing inside the structural type system through type-ids that values acquire when they are constructed.

must_cover.text: Explain that distinct types provide functionality similar to nominal (branded) types within Ballerina's structural type system, so two structurally identical distinct types are different types
Declare distinct error types such as `type NotFound distinct error;` and test them with `e is NotFound`, so errors with the same shape but different type-ids can be told apart
Declare distinct object types with `distinct object { ... }` and distinct classes with `distinct class C { ... }`, knowing `distinct` applies only to object and error types
Explain that `distinct T` requires T to be definite and a subtype of object or error, contains only values of T whose type-ids include this occurrence's type-id, and is always a proper subtype of T

Describe a type-id's parts, namely a module id (organization, module name, platform parts), a local id that is the defined type or class name when it is the only `distinct` in that definition or otherwise a compiler-generated integer, and a public flag
Explain that an object or error value's set of type-ids is fixed when it is constructed, is part of its shape, and is split into primary and secondary type-ids

Explain that object and error values must be constructed from a definite type descriptor, which induces their type-ids; `error` and object type descriptors are definite, and an intersection of definite types induces the union of their type-ids
Use an intersection of distinct error types such as `type E1E2 E1 & E2;` to describe errors that carry the type-ids of both, and construct them with `error E1E2("msg")`
Explain that `distinct T` has its own type-id as primary and T's type-ids as secondary, and that a distinct class's included object types contribute secondary type-ids
Explain that it is an error for a type reference or object type inclusion to induce a non-public type-id from another module
Inspect a type's type-ids at runtime with `typedesc:typeIds(td)`, optionally only the primary ones

out_of_scope: Error values and the error constructor in general (concept.errors)
Classes and object type inclusion in general (concept.classes, concept.objects)
nodes.notes: 5.6.1 says 'A type-reference referring to a type descriptor T is definite if and only if T.' — word missing ('T is definite'). In error_intersection_type_ids, constructing via an intersection type reference is allowed per 6.17 ('it is allowed for E to refer to an intersection-type-descriptor').

nodes.title: Type narrowing
nodes.summary: How the compiler narrows the static type of a local variable or parameter from boolean conditions (occurrence typing) and from statements that cannot complete normally.

must_cover.text: Narrow a union-typed local variable or parameter with `if x is T { ... } else { ... }`, where x has type `Tx & T` in the if block and the read-only difference of Tx and T in the else block

Explain the read-only difference used for the false case, where a mutable part of the type is removed only if it is entirely contained in T, because a mutable value can look like T without belonging to it
Narrow with `x == E` and `x != E` when E has a singleton simple type, e.g. `if x == () { ... }` or `if x != () { ... }` to remove nil
Combine narrowings with `!`, `&&` and `||`, e.g. `x is int && x > 0` uses the narrowed type in the right operand, and `!(x is int)` swaps the true and false narrowings

Identify where narrowed types apply, namely the right operand of `&&` (truth) and `||` (falsity), the branches of `? :`, the blocks of `if`/`else`, the body of `while`, the block of a match clause after its guard, and all clauses after a query `where` clause

Use narrowing from normal completion, e.g. after `if x is error { return x; }` the variable x excludes error for the rest of the block, because a statement that cannot complete normally implies `never`

Explain that after `if E B1 else B2` the narrowed type is the union of the types implied by normal completion of B1 and B2, that a missing `else` acts like an empty block, and `else if` is treated as a nested if-else

Explain that narrowing stops applying where the variable may have been assigned since the condition was evaluated, and that it is a compile error if an assignment inside a `while`, `foreach` or query action body would invalidate a narrowing from outside the loop
Know that conditional narrowing is defined only for local variables and parameters referenced by name in the condition, so to narrow a field value first copy it into a local variable
Use a wildcard destructuring assignment such as `Z _ = v;` in the final else to assert that all union cases were handled, so adding a new member to the union later causes a compile error
Recognize that a `match` on a variable narrows it in each clause to the target type read-only-intersected with what the clause's patterns can match after excluding earlier unguarded clauses

nodes.notes: 7.12 'If E has the form E1 && E2' defines T1 as 'narrowed type implied by the truth of T1' (should read E1); similar letter slips appear in the && rule.

nodes.title: Typedesc
nodes.summary: Runtime type descriptor values of type `typedesc<T>`, obtained from type names and `typeof`, and used to drive dependently-typed functions.

must_cover.text: Use `typedesc<T>` for immutable values representing resolved type descriptors, where a typedesc belongs to `typedesc<T>` iff the type it describes is a subtype of T (so typedesc is covariant), and plain `typedesc` contains all of them
Obtain a typedesc value by referencing a type or class name in an expression, e.g. `typedesc<Person> td = Person;`
Explain that a type descriptor may carry value-construction information (such as default values) and annotations that are resolved at runtime, which a typedesc value represents
Use `typeof expr` to get a typedesc for the runtime type of a value, whose static type is `typedesc<T>` for an expression of static type T
Explain that `typeof` on a simple value yields a singleton type of that value, with no annotations, and a new typedesc value on each evaluation

Explain that `typeof` on a reference value returns the type descriptor used to construct it (the inherent type for containers, a singleton type for immutable containers, the class for objects), identical for repeated evaluations, including any annotations on that descriptor
Call dependently-typed functions whose return type refers to a `typedesc` parameter, such as `value:cloneWithType(v, Person)` returning `Person|error`
Rely on an inferred typedesc default `typedesc<anydata> t = <>`, where the caller infers the argument from the contextually expected type, e.g. `Person p = check v.cloneWithType();`
Use `typedesc:typeIds(t, primaryOnly)` to get the readonly array of `typedesc:TypeId` records (module id and local id) induced by a typedesc, or nil if the type is not definite
Explain that typedesc values are inherently immutable and therefore always belong to `readonly`

out_of_scope: Declaring parameters and defaults in general (concept.functions)
nodes.notes: 6.21 ends with 'For an error, this is the same as the type descriptor used in the functional-constructor-expr' — a stale term for error-constructor-expr.

nodes.title: Unions and intersections
nodes.summary: Type descriptors that describe subsets of the existing values, such as unions, optional types, singleton types, any, never and intersections.

must_cover.text: Explain that these type descriptors add no new values to the universe; they only describe subsets of existing values
Declare union types such as `int|string`, whose shapes are the union of the members' shapes, and use them for variables and parameters that accept several types
Use optional types `T?`, which are exactly equivalent to `T|()`
Define singleton types from constant expressions, such as `"GET"|"POST"` or `1|2|3`, each containing exactly one shape
Explain that a singleton type referencing a structured constant contains only values with the read-only bit set, so a mutable value never belongs to a singleton type
Use `any` for every value except errors, know that `any|error` covers all values, and that a list or mapping containing error members still belongs to `any`
Use `never` for the empty type, for example as the return type of a function that never returns or in `xml<never>` for the empty xml value, and know `T|never` is the same as `T`
Write intersection types `T1 & T2` whose shapes are in both types, most commonly `readonly & T`, and know an intersection that denotes an empty set of shapes is a compile error
Explain that intersecting two function types is an error unless a single function type descriptor is a subtype of both
Explain that `T1|T2` and `T1&T2` are not classes and cannot be used with `new`, even when T1 or T2 is a class
Explain that for `R & readonly` with a record type R, a field default whose closure returns a Cloneable value is wrapped to apply ImmutableClone, and otherwise the field loses its default
Explain that `any` is not definite and a union is definite only if its members are definite and induce the same type-ids, which matters when constructing objects or errors from the expected type

out_of_scope: The readonly type and read-only bit (concept.mutability_readonly)

nodes.title: Value cloning
nodes.summary: The Cloneable type, deep copying with `clone` and `cloneReadOnly` (Clone and ImmutableClone), and constructing a value of a specified type with `cloneWithType`.

must_cover.text: Use the `value:Cloneable` type, defined as `readonly|xml|Cloneable[]|map<Cloneable>|table<map<Cloneable>>`, as the domain of the cloning operations
Use `v.clone()` to make a deep copy of structured and sequence values that keeps the same inherent types and returns immutable values (and immutable subtrees) without copying them
Explain that Clone preserves the graph of references, so shared members stay shared, cycles are reproduced and cloning a cyclic value terminates
Use `v.cloneReadOnly()` to get a deep immutable copy of type `T & readonly`, where every newly constructed value has its read-only bit on and already-immutable values are not copied

Explain the ImmutableClone operation, which preserves graph structure including cycles by building the whole graph before making it immutable, and is used implicitly for error detail fields and annotation values
Rely on `x.clone() == x` being true for every anydata value x
Know that calls to `clone` and `cloneReadOnly` are always isolated expressions, so they can be used to safely transfer values into or out of `lock` statements

Use `v.cloneWithType(T)` or `T x = check v.cloneWithType();` to construct a value of a specified anydata type by deep copy, where inherent types and read-only bits come from T, for a union the leftmost workable member is used, and missing record fields are filled from defaults

Explain how cloneWithType differs from clone: the result is always a tree, so it returns an error on cyclic input, immutable structural values are copied, and numeric values are converted with NumericConvert
Explain that a worker send applies Clone to the message value, so the receiver gets a copy rather than a shared reference

nodes.title: Variables
nodes.summary: Declaring local and module-level variables, how var inference, final and definite assignment work, how identifiers are scoped, and let expressions.

must_cover.text: Declare local variables with an initializer, e.g. `int count = 0;`, whose scope starts immediately after the statement and ends at the end of the enclosing block, with the declared type providing the contextually expected type for the initializer

Use `var` to infer a local variable's type from its initializer, knowing the broad type is inferred (e.g. `var s = "x";` has type `string`) unless the declaration is `final`, in which case the precise type (here the singleton `"x"`) is used
Declare `final` local variables that must not be assigned after the declaration, and explain that `final` is not deep: a final variable can hold a mutable value

Declare a local variable without an initializer, e.g. `string label;`, and satisfy definite assignment: the compiler must be able to verify it is assigned on every path before each reference; if `final` it may be assigned at most once, and its type must not be `never`

Explain block scope: a block-scope declaration may hide a module-scope declaration of the same identifier, but it is a compile error for two block-scope declarations of the same identifier in the same symbol space to have overlapping scopes

Distinguish the main symbol space (variables, constants, types, functions), the prefix symbol space (import and xmlns prefixes) and the annotation-tag symbol space, knowing block scope has no annotation-tag symbol space

Declare module-level variables such as `int counter = 0;` or `public final string NAME = "x";`, whose scope is the whole module, knowing a `public` module variable must not use `var` and a `final` one cannot be assigned after initialization

Declare a module variable without an initializer, e.g. `int[] cache;`, which must be initialized in the module's `init` function and definitely assigned at every reference; its type must not be `never`
Explain that `var` in a module variable declaration infers the precise type when the declaration is `final` and the broad type otherwise

Declare an `isolated` module variable, which must not be `public`, must bind a plain variable name and must have an isolated initializer expression, and know it can be accessed only within a `lock` statement

Reference variables, parameters, constants, functions, types and classes by name in expressions, including qualified references such as `mod:name`, knowing a reference to a type or class evaluates to a typedesc value

Use let expressions such as `let int x = f() in x * x` and `let var a = 1, var b = 2 in a + b`, where the bound variables are in scope only in the expression after `in` and multiple declarations are equivalent to nested lets

Explain that variables bound by a let expression are implicitly final, that `var` in a let-var-decl infers the precise static type of the initializer, and that the typed binding pattern must be guaranteed by static types to match

out_of_scope: The isolation rules behind isolated variables (concept.isolation)
nodes.notes: When an isolated-qual could be parsed as part of module-init-var-quals or of a typed-binding-pattern (an isolated object type), the spec chooses the qualifier parse; not made into an item.

nodes.title: Worker messages
nodes.summary: Sending and receiving Cloneable messages between peer workers with async send, sync send, flush, and single, multiple and alternate receive actions.

must_cover.text: Know that a worker message must belong to `value:Cloneable` and that the sent value is copied with the Clone operation
Send messages only between peer workers: a function's default worker (referred to as `function`) and its named workers are peers, and the workers of one fork statement are peers of each other
Send a message without waiting for it to be received with the async send action `expr -> w;`, which evaluates to `()`
Use the sync send action `expr ->> w`, which is equivalent to an async send followed by `flush w` and so may evaluate to the receiver's failure error

Use `flush w` (or `flush` alone for every peer) to wait until previously sent messages are received; it evaluates to `()` or to the receiver's error if the receiver terminated with failure, and panics if the receiver panicked
Receive a message with `T v = <- w;`, whose static type combines the message type, `error:NoMessage` when the matching send might not run, and the sender's failure error type
Receive from several workers at once with `<- {a: w1, b: w2}` (or `<- {w1, w2}`), producing a record of the received values, or an `error:NoMessage` if any expected message was never sent
Use the alternate receive action `<- w1 | w2` (new in 2024R1) to take the first non-error message from several workers, getting `error:NoMessage` if none of them sent one
Know that if the sending worker terminated with failure before sending, the receive evaluates to that error, and if it terminated abnormally (panic) the receive panics

Explain that each send and receive is matched to a queue slot at compile time, in syntactic order, so send and receive actions cannot appear where they could run more than once, such as inside a loop body

Know that a send action may sit in a branch that never runs (2024R1 removed the requirement that every send must be executed), in which case the receiver gets `error:NoMessage`, whereas a receive action may not be placed in such a conditional context
Know that an async send whose receiver may terminate with failure is a compile-time error unless a sync send or flush is guaranteed to run before the sender terminates successfully

Know that a worker about to terminate normally waits until its outgoing messages have been received (or the receiver has terminated), and terminates abnormally with the receiver's value if the receiver panicked

nodes.notes: Spec typo in 7.8.1.3: the prose says 'A sync-send-action `E -> R` is equivalent to an async-send-action `E ->> R` followed by a flush', swapping the arrows. The grammar defines async-send-action as `expression -> peer-worker ;` and sync-send-action as `expression ->> peer-worker`; items follow the grammar.

nodes.title: XML
nodes.summary: The xml sequence type with its element, processing instruction, comment and text items, xml<T> types, xml template expressions, concatenation, mutability and storage identity.

must_cover.text: Explain that an xml value is a sequence of element, processing instruction, comment and text items, that a single item is itself a sequence, and that the empty xml value is distinct from `""` and `()`
Use the built-in subtypes `xml:Element`, `xml:ProcessingInstruction`, `xml:Comment` and `xml:Text`, knowing that `xml:Text` also includes the empty xml value

Use `xml<T>` for sequences whose items all belong to `T` (e.g. `xml<xml:Element>`), and know that `xml<xml<T>>` equals `xml<T>`, `xml<xml:Text>` equals `xml:Text`, and `xml<never>` is just the empty value
Explain that consecutive text items are merged when an xml value is constructed, so an xml value never contains two adjacent text items
Describe an element as a name string, an attributes map of type `map<string>` and children of type `xml`
Explain that element, processing instruction and comment singletons have storage identity while text items and longer sequences do not, and that a sequence compares with `===` item by item

Explain that `xml:Text` is inherently immutable, elements, processing instructions and comments are selectively immutable, a multi-item sequence is read-only only if all its items are, and a read-only element has read-only attributes and children
Explain that mutable items of an xml value can be mutated but the number and identity of its constituents, and the identity of an element attributes map, are fixed at construction

Construct xml with templates such as `xml `<book id="${id}">${title}</book>``, which are parsed as XML content with interpolations allowed only in character data and attribute values (not namespace attributes)

Explain that attribute interpolations must be non-nil simple types (expected type `string`), content interpolations may be `xml` or a non-nil simple type converted to a string, and each evaluation makes a new copy with interpolations evaluated in order
Explain that an xml template inside a constant expression constructs a read-only xml value
Concatenate xml with `x1 + x2` (no copying of constituents), and with strings, where a non-empty string acts as a text item and an empty string yields the xml operand unchanged
Iterate over the items of an `xml<T>` value with `foreach`, each iteration value being a singleton of type `T`
Use `lang.xml` functions such as `elements`, `children`, `getName`, `getAttributes`, `getChildren`, `data`, `createElement` and `fromString` through method-call syntax

nodes.notes: 6.6.2 says the contextually expected type for content interpolations is xml, but a non-xml simple-typed value is still accepted and converted to a string (not an error).

nodes.title: XML namespaces
nodes.summary: How XML element and attribute names are represented as expanded names, how namespace attributes are kept and synthesized, and how xmlns declarations bind prefixes at block and module level.

must_cover.text: Explain that element and attribute names are expanded-name strings of the form `{namespace-uri}local-name`, or just the local name when there is no namespace
Declare namespace prefixes in a block with `xmlns "http://example.com/ns" as ex;`, or a default namespace by omitting `as`, where the URI is a simple constant expression of type string
Declare module-level `xmlns` declarations, which apply only to the source part in which they occur, like imports
Explain that the prefixes and default namespace declared by `xmlns` declarations are the in-scope namespaces used when xml templates are processed
Explain that `ex:local` with an xmlns-declared prefix evaluates to the expanded name string `{uri}local`

Explain that xmlns prefixes share a symbol space with import module prefixes, separate from the main symbol space, and that `xmlns` is predeclared as `http://www.w3.org/2000/xmlns/` and cannot be redeclared
Explain that an element attributes map also holds its namespace declarations, whose keys start with `{http://www.w3.org/2000/xmlns/}`

Explain that namespace attributes are synthesized for prefixes (other than `xml` and the default namespace) that are used by an element or its attributes but not declared on it, so prefixes survive when the element is extracted

Describe how converting xml to an infoset for serialization prunes redundant namespace declarations, uses the `xml` prefix for the XML namespace, reuses or generates prefixes and adds `xmlns=""` to undeclare an inherited default namespace
Use the `lang.xml` constants `xml:XML_NAMESPACE_URI`, `xml:XMLNS_NAMESPACE_URI` and the expanded-name constants `xml:lang`, `xml:space` and `xml:base`

out_of_scope: Name patterns with prefixes in navigation expressions (concept.xml_navigation)
nodes.notes: 5.3.2.1 serialization rules are long and implementation-oriented; marked advanced.

nodes.title: XML navigation
nodes.summary: Attribute access with `.` and `?.` on xml values, and XPath-like filter and step expressions using xml name patterns.

must_cover.text: Read an attribute with `e.id`, of static type `string|error`, which returns an error when the value is not a singleton element (including when it is empty) or the attribute is missing
Read an attribute with `e?.id`, of static type `string|error|()`, which returns `()` for an empty xml value or a missing attribute and an error when the value is not a singleton element
Name attributes with a plain identifier, an xmlns-prefixed name expanded at compile time to `{uri}local`, or a module-qualified string constant such as `xml:lang`
Write xml name patterns `*`, `name`, `ns:name`, `ns:*` and alternatives `a|b`, where an unprefixed name means a name in the in-scope default namespace if one is declared
Select element items whose name matches a pattern with `x.<book>`, of static type `xml<xml:Element>`
Use `x/*` to get the children of every element in `x`, equivalent to mapping `xml:getChildren` over `xml:elements(x)`
Use `x/<title>` to get the element children matching a name pattern
Use `x/**/<title>` to get the matching element descendants, based on `xml:getDescendants`

Extend steps with `.

`, `[i]` and `.method(args)`, which apply to the result for each element, e.g. `x/[0]`

Explain that ambiguity with member access and method calls is resolved by including as much as possible in the xml step expression, and that navigation needs an operand whose static type is a subtype of xml

nodes.notes: 6.12: for the required form, every case where the optional form gives () becomes an error, including an empty xml operand.

edges.note: type names and literals are built from lexical tokens
each basic type has a corresponding lang library module
numeric literal typing uses the contextually expected type
XML step expressions are defined in terms of xml:map, xml:elements, xml:getChildren and xml:getDescendants
